speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was a member of the committee which unanimously approved this bill. I might say that this unanimity is not always present in the committee, the members of which include the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Essex East, but in this case there was unanimity.
My purpose in rising is to express my satisfaction at what the government has done and also to try to put on record certain views, including certain statements by witnesses and people whose opinions are of value, so that these may be useful to those who will continue to assist the government in creating a stronger and stronger feeling toward our duties and responsibilities in assisting underdeveloped countries. In this connection I am hardly bold enough to hope I can interest the press. One of these days somebody will come along who will be of interest to the press, but
5112	HOUSE OF
International Development Association I shall put the evidence of these witnesses on record in the sincere belief that it will be useful.
First of all I would like to go to our own Prime Minister, one of the world figures of today, and quote a statement I quoted some time ago. The Prime Minister, has said:
Economic assistance to underdeveloped countries is a major and mandatory need if freedom is to be preserved in the world.
Then I was delighted to observe the other day that while the Prime Minister was attending DePauw University he followed up that statement with this one, and I quote briefly from his words on that occasion. He gives certain statistics, and then he says:
I do not need, in view of these statistics, to underline the arguments for sacrifice on the part of the industrialized countries in the field of economic assistance-
Then finally he says:
There is no alternative to continuing with, even increasing, this type of international assistance and co-operation. Until the day comes when the less developed nations expand their capacity to trade and achieve self-sustaining growth, there is an unanswerable argument in favour of assisting them. It was with this argument in mind that, at the recent meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in London, it was decided to begin work on a program of economic aid to the emerging nations of Africa, the largest remaining area where International assistance has yet to be launched on a scale remotely consistent with present and future needs.
It has been made quite clear in the press that our own Prime Minister was a leader in connection with this movement for aid to Africa, and I am glad to think that is so.
I should like to quote briefly from a pamphlet by Paul Hoffman which I commend to all members, which is called "One Hundred Countries, One And One Quarter Billion People". In the first place he draws attention to what I feel is a very important point, namely-

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ARTICLES OF AGREEMENT AND PAYMENT OF SUBSCRIPTION
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I think the hon. member who is now speaking ought to be accorded the courtesy which his sense of responsibility and the seriousness of this matter warrant. We ought to have the opportunity of hearing what he has to say.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ARTICLES OF AGREEMENT AND PAYMENT OF SUBSCRIPTION
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member, I can assure hon. members that what I am saying is just as dull to me as it is to them. I quote from Paul Hoffman, who has this to say:
There was a time not long ago when, everywhere in the world, resources were for the most part exploited rather than developed.
Then he goes on to say this:
These attitudes and practices have changed markedly. Exploitation is widely recognized as shortsighted and self-defeating.


Not long ago, it was unquestioned that "the poor are always with us," and poverty of the majority of the people in any country-and certainly in the world-was regarded as inevitable, to be alleviated, as far as possible, through charity. Only in the last 30 or 40 years have even the most advanced countries of the west accepted that a national society, operating through government, has the responsibility for creating conditions which spur economic development within its borders, relieve poverty, and raise the standard of living of all classes in the population.
Today they are discovering that the same principles and similar methods work on a world scale, and that they yield similar beneficial results.
Then I shall quote a word or two from Mr. Hoffman dealing with his own proposal:
My proposal is this: That we-all of us together- fix it as our goal to double in the 1960's, as compared with the 1950's, the annual per capita rate of economic growth in 100 countries and territories containing a billion and a quarter of the world's people. If we achieve this goal it will mean increasing the per capita economic growth rate of the less developed countries from an average of 1 per cent a year in the 1950's to an average of 2 per cent in the 1960's.
You will see that this is a rather modest objective he sets. Then I wish to quote what Hoffman has to say about the subject we are discussing now, that is the international development association. He speaks very warmly about it:
A splendid first virtue of the proposed I.D.A. as an instrument for promoting economic development in the low income countries is that it will be a genuinely co-operative undertaking comprising, as members, both industrialized and underdeveloped countries. All members will make contributions; all will have a voice in the truly international administration that will result.
I should like to accentuate as best I can the fact that Mr. Hoffman and other competent people who have been close to this question stress again and again that this is a matter of investment and not charity; that the nations requiring assistance have to take the initiative themselves, in effect have to become creditworthy. It is not just the question of dishing out money to undeserving people, but a question of assisting people to help themselves. I continue:
A second great virtue of the proposed I.D.A is that, inasmuch as the world bank has gained universal renown as an efficient and effective and objective international financial institution, I.D.A., as an affiliate of the world bank, will borrow its accumulated experience, knowledge, and expert direction.
A third virtue of I.D.A. is that it is not required to confine its loans to support of specific projects, but may extend its support to plans and programs that support economic development.
This outstanding man is known to most hon. members. He is the man who administered the Marshall plan which was such a brilliant success. He goes on to say:
There is, nevertheless, a major shortcoming in the international development association as currently projected:

The authorization planned for I.D.A. is only $1 billion. One billion dollars over five years! This is obviously too little to come anywhere near meeting the minimum investment gap of $2 billion a year. And yet, there is no other institution either in existence or on the drawing boards that can take up the slack!
For this reason I welcome the fact that in the bill it is proposed that the amount contemplated shall be reviewed and, if necessary, increased. Here we have the statements of Mr. Hoffman, who has worked very hard to find out what is required. He strongly praises the I.D.A. but points out what is required.
I should like now to quote from a statement made by Adlai Stevenson which appeared in the magazine Foreign Affairs of January, 1960. I shall quote two short paragraphs from Mr. Stevenson's most interesting article:
To me the two most dangerous realities we now face are the multiplication of nuclear weapons and the disparity in living standards between the rich nations and the poor.
I will not read further from -that section of his remarks but I wanted to bring that sentence to the attention of hon. members. Further along he writes:
The average annual income in the United States is more than $2,000 as against less than $100 for a third of the world's population. And the worst thing about this disparity is that the rich nations are getting richer and the poor poorer.
That is the opinion of a man with a world reputation. I think it is full of practical good sense. I like to remind myself that he is not merely a man of good common sense but was also the good governor of one of the largest states in the United States. He goes on to speak about figures:
Happily, there is, at long last, a growing realization here and among our friends that these are the decisive areas and that we must assist the underdeveloped peoples to advance to self-sustaining growth while preserving their independence and some hope of evolving a political democracy. Without an alternative to communist methods of development, we face grim prospects indeed in poor countries where literacy is low, hunger high and the gap between resources and population widening.
I wish to read just one sentence of a speech made by Mr. Eugene R. Black at Oxford University on March 3 last. He is the banker who has lent some $5 billion on business terms without loss. In one paragraph he outlines the responsibility that must be taken by those who wish to benefit. He says, for example:
How important it is to develop a pride of workmanship so that every ounce of resources available for promoting higher material living standards is used as efficiently as possible.
I hope that will convey to every hon. member an idea of the responsibility that he is laying on the underdeveloped countries.
79951-0-323J
International Development Association He then goes on to utter a sentence every word of which I commend to hon. members.
And how important it is that the free world community stand ready to pledge whatever measure of its wealth can be usefully absorbed in this endeavour.
He is not asking us to waste our money but to pledge whatever measure of wealth can be usefully absorbed in this endeavour. Mr. Black is a hard-headed banker and I suppose knows more about these world-wide problems than any other man on the planet. I remind hon. gentlemen of the contribution Mr. Black made to the solution of the problems of the Indus waters.
I wish now to quote a sentence or two from a well-known writer in the London Economist; Barbara Ward, one of the most brilliant people living. She made a statement which I think really puts us on the spot. If we agree with it then we must do something about it. If some do not agree with it, that is their privilege. This is what she said:
As the world enters the 1960's, one fact seems sure. The pace of revolutionary change, in every sphere of human affairs will gather momentum.
The breakthrough accomplished in the fifties in weapons, in space research, in every type of scientific advance; the political breakthrough of a score of new nations; the emotional breakthrough of a third of humanity hungering for economic growth -all these forces will expand explosively to make the sixties a period of challenge and change unequalled in human history.
What, in these circumstances will be the response of the western powers? The answer depends not only upon the new political leadership available in the west, it depends profoundly upon the sort of people the free nations have become as they face the mounting crises of their age.

speechtext: The hon. member does not identify his quotation. Is that from her lectures at the University of Ghana?

speechtext:
That statement is from the New York Times of December, 1959. I should like now to make a brief reference to a remark made by a man who I believe is familiar to us all, Sir Douglas Copland. He was the Australian representative here for years. In a proposal reported in the Globe and Mail of June 8, 1960, he stated:
Canada and Australia should give leadership in assisting underdeveloped countries.
Thank goodness we in Canada have given some leadership. Then he went on to speak about the question of trade. Hoffman has very strongly made the point that aid makes trade. That is a point which Hoffman underlines. Sir Douglas Copland goes pretty far in referring to the subject. He suggests:
There is no reason-why the western world should not contribute perhaps 1 per cent of its national income to underdeveloped countries.

International Development Association
Some people will think that is a lot. The statement to which I really wish to direct hon. members' attention is this:
To some people a suggestion that 1 per cent of national income should be set aside as a contribution to underdeveloped countries will be regarded as a cost. This is far from being the case. It should be regarded as an investment from which the return will be very high.
I think it is terribly important for us to understand that. If we believe that statement it will take us a long way.
I will read another short paragraph from Hoffman which I think is full of practical good sense.
The expression "trade and aid," which is used so often these days, conveys the subtly misleading impression that "trade" and "aid" are separate entities, that they might be mixed in varying proportions in promoting development in the low income countries, and even that one might be substituted for the other. This is, of course, false. Aid is trade. Investment is trade. The dollars or pounds or francs or marks that are expended on foreign aid and investment in the low income countries are only symbols representing food, textiles, metals, machinery, and other manufactures produced in the industrialized countries and exported to the developing countries, and technical services made available to them in support of their development. Aid and investment abroad is therefore more than trade; it is production and employment both in the investing and in the recipient countries; and it is economic growth and increased prosperity all around.
Once we get this idea fixed in our heads, we can banish the idea that aid to and investment in the underdeveloped countries is charity or that it is a one-way street.
I commend those words to hon. gentlemen. I might say that this pamphlet is available, and I suggest that everyone should read it. It is packed full of practical good sense from a man who without exaggeration has to his credit the fact that he set western Europe on its feet.
I am almost finished now, Mr. Chairman. I wanted to put forward these things which I have read to you. I suggest that people have a choice. Needless to say, those people to whom I have referred know what they are talking about. It is not a lot of hooey but sober practical common sense. If you believe these things then the answer is you have to do something about it.
We have done something about it. I read to you what Mr. Hoffman said in welcoming the I.D.A., suggesting that that is what is implied in the act itself, because he leaves the door open for additional funds. I suggest that these words are weighty words. I suggest that what Barbara Ward said about those explosive questions facing us in 1960 is a simple statement of fact, and if it is a simple statement of fact we cannot run away from it. I suggest that in the past this nation to which we belong, when it has been faced

with something that was regarded as a real emergency, has always stood up to it.
I do beg that you who are leaders in your communities, who are here responsible for legislation, who are approving this legislation, which is a fine step in the right direction; having heard the words of our own Prime Minister and of other people; having heard the words of those practical men who have been doing things in this matter; having heard what to me was a very good idea, that exploitation is receding and investment developing may not remain inactive but may do something about it.
I was anxious to bring these things forward. I hope the witnesses I have called and their words may carry much further than mine. If they do, I have not wasted your time.

speechtext: I should like to lend my wholehearted support to the efforts of the hon. member for Greenwood in creating public interest in this matter of support for underdeveloped countries. I do not wish to take up the time of the commitee except to assure the hon. member for Greenwood and this committee that my support is with him.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ARTICLES OF AGREEMENT AND PAYMENT OF SUBSCRIPTION
speechtext:
All I want to say at this time in support of the bill is to place on record the fact that while we are asked by the terms of this bill to authorize Canada's participation to the extent of $37.83 million, under the articles of agreement of the international development association our obligation initially is going to be only 10 per cent of our initial subscription. In other words we are obligated to spend within the next number of months only the sum of $3,783,000. We cannot let the people of Canada believe that we are now investing $37.83 million in this field of international aid. All we are doing is investing $3,783,000. Then we have about an equal amount which is payable one year later, and another similar amount one year after that. I feel that, much as we welcome this move, it should not be misunderstood by the Canadian people that we are immediately about to invest $37.83 million, because the articles of agreement allow us a goodly number of years in which to pay our full original subscription of $37.83 million.
When he replies, I should like the minister to indicate whether there has been any approach made in the evolution of this organization to obtain the co-operation and the participation of nations behind the so-called iron curtain. I feel it most regrettable that in the matter of international aid we are continuing to grant this aid as a western bloc, while the countries behind the iron curtain are granting their forms of aid in their own way. If the word "international" in the bill means anything at all it ought to

mean that this is international indeed. I regret that political implications are involved and are being used in so many of our international aid programs. I should like to have a little bit of an accounting on whether any of these countries have been asked to participate-I mean the so-called iron curtain countries-and what their reaction has been.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a word on behalf of our party in support of this bill, which was given very careful and sympathetic consideration in a committee of this house. Although I was not a member of that committee I have had the opportunity of reading the record of its proceedings and, as my hon. friend from Greenwood in his very constructive and thoughtful observations of a few moments ago pointed out, in respect of this matter there seems to be unanimity in the house.
The purposes of the bill are such, of course, that they must, I think, commend it to all of us. The committee report quotes Mr. Ras-minsky, who is familiar with these matters, as having stated its purposes by reading article I of the bill, namely that:
The purposes of the association are to promote economic development, increase productivity and thus raise standards of living in the less-developed areas of the world included within the association's membership.
At one time there were those who had some hesitation about the possibility of realizing these purposes through this association without causing some overlapping or some confusion and, indeed, without having some result of which we in Canada perhaps would not entirely approve. However, I think the justification for the association has been the great difference between the loans that are to be made under this association and those made by the bank itself. As was pointed out by Mr. Rasminsky and, indeed, as has already been pointed out by the minister, the terms would be somewhat easier in connection with loans under the I.D.A., and therefore loans could be made for economic development under the I.D.A. which perhaps should not be made under the bank as it is constituted at present. I think that does indeed justify the establishment of this association.
The hesitation which I know members of the government may have had when the association was first put forward have been removed in a way which Mr. Rasminsky and the minister have already pointed out. Particularly there is the hesitation and doubt once felt-and perhaps we may also have some questions to ask about this when we deal with the clauses of the bill-about the possibility of using this fund for United States surplus disposal programs in a way which

International Development Association we could not support. That is one doubt which was very much in all our minds at the time and which, so far as the government is concerned, has been removed.
The purposes of the bill, as I have said, are such that they commend themselves to all of us. They represent a further effort to meet what the hon. member for Greenwood has just referred to as a major and mandatory need. In the efforts that are being made internationally to meet this need, I think the time has come when we have to be careful that we do not proliferate our international agencies for this purpose. We have a good many now, and perhaps we should be more careful in the future than we have been in the past about relating the work of all these organizations, international in scope under the United Nations and under the Colombo plan arrangement, so as to make sure that they do not get in each other's may.
The need is great and, as the hon. member for Greenwood has pointed out, the need is not decreasing but increasing. I think he quoted that figure that Adlai Stevenson put forward in a speech not long ago of a requirement of $5 billion a year by way of assistance from what we call the developed countries to meet the needs of economic development in what we call the underdeveloped countries. The gap between the developed countries and these underdeveloped countries is not lessening in this respect but is widening. In other words the need is growing, not diminishing, in spite of the acceptance of reponsibility by the developed countries to do what they can to meet that need. That in itself is an encouraging development, because I think this is the first time in history that the more fortunate nations have accepted formally, through international organizations, a responsibility for helping the underdeveloped and less fortunate countries.
But the need is great and is increasing. I read not long ago-I think I am right in my memory of the figures-that. the per capita increase in the national income of the United States over a recent period of a few years- I cannot remember the exact period-was greater than the total per capita income of many of the Asian and African countries. We are perhaps falling behind in meeting this necessity rather than gaining in meeting the requirements that are before us. In other words, we are falling behind in the race between resources and existence in so many countries.
The purposes of aid are, of course, just as important as the aid itself. That is why it is of such great importance to have aid of this kind, whenever possible, given under the United Nations where the political fears, suspicions,

International Development Association pressures and influences just referred to need not exist. Surely aid under the United Nations should be above suspicion. When the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam talks about the undesirability of any political strings being attached to western aid he is, of course, quite right; but aid under the United Nations does not and need not have these suspicions associated with it.
While all countries in the west may not be above suspicion in these matters, surely the record of the west and the record of the United States in what has been done to help meet these needs bear comparison not only in quantity but in purpose and in manner of distribution with the aid from the U.S.S.R. and countries behind the iron curtain. I know there have been some instances where aid from the U.S.S.R. has been very carefully proposed and as carefully administered to give the impression that there was no political purpose attached to it in any way, shape or form. That has happened in some cases, but in other cases the connection between politics and aid from the U.S.S.R. has been open and blatant.
I am thinking particularly of the help the U.S.S.R. once gave Yugoslavia. Immediately Yugoslavia refused to buckle down to Soviet foreign policy, that aid was cut off without a trace. So while it is desirable to remove from aid any political purposes of the kind that have been mentioned, I think this kind of proposal does just that. If the Soviet union and its friends criticize the United States, particularly, for tying up aid to political purposes, even under the United Nations, it should not be forgotten that any time the Soviet union so desires it can join in this kind of United Nations activity. So far it has not shown much desire to do so. Perhaps that is the most effective commentary on the criticism which we do get at times from the U.S.S.R.
The question of keeping international aid out of politics has a bearing on whether it should be in the form of grants or in the form of loans. That is why there is a good deal to be said for increasing our aid of this type under the development association and under the world bank in contrast to direct grants, some of which, while no doubt welcomed by the countries receiving them, do carry with them a kind of stigma of charity which no self-respecting people wish to have attached even to the kind of help they are getting from countries like our own. Therefore this kind of assistance under the international development association has that to commend it. It is the kind of assistance that could not be criticized on any of the political grounds mentioned this morning.


I think that is all I need to say now, Mr. Chairman. When we come to detailed discussion of the bill we may have some questions to ask. Meanwhile I want to repeat what the hon. member for Essex East has already said on second reading, that we are wholeheartedly behind the purposes of the bill, that we think it is well designed to carry out these purposes, and that this is a very appropriate contribution for Canada to make.

The article which contemplates the possible use of such funds is article III, which is divided into two sections. The first section deals with additions to the resources in the form of additional subscriptions. Additional subscriptions may be made under decision of the association only by a two thirds majority of the total voting power.
Section 2 of this article deals with the provision of supplementary resources by a member in the currency of another member. This is the provision under which it might be possible for a country like the United States, holding a substantial amount of currency of other countries, to seek to offer these sums in foreign currency to the association for its use. I point out that such sums could only be accepted in that case by a decision of the association. That decision would not require a two thirds majority, but a simple majority in the ordinary way. No country has a right to make additional subscriptions to the association merely by turning over large sums of foreign currencies which it holds. This can be done, I emphasize, only by a decision of the association itself. The acceptance of such funds by the association does not give any additional voting rights to the country that has subscribed this foreign currency. It gives it a right, in that event, only to receive a special development certificate.
Then there is a further safeguard in subclause (c) of section 2 which reads:
Nothing in this section shall preclude the association from accepting resources from a member in its own currency on such terms as may be agreed upon.
I stress the fact that the matter is left under the control of the association. The United States subscribes, in round figures, about 32 per cent of the total capital. In so far as what is likely to happen is concerned, I think that is best summarized by Mr. Rasminsky in that passage of his testimony recorded on page 25, which followed the quotation to which the hon. member for Essex East referred concerning the statement by the national advisory council. Mr. Rasminsky followed with this statement:
I would not say that was an enthusiastic statement of possibilities. X cannot guarantee, of course, that the American hopes and aspirations are the same as ours in this connection, but against the background of the whole record of these discussions I think that the management of the institutions will be quite cautious about bringing proposals forward regarding these supplementary contributions.
I think it is quite clear that if any proposal is made to ask the association to accept counterpart funds in pursuance of section 2 of article III, the Canadian representative would wish to give such proposals very strict scrutiny.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, if I correctly followed the remarks of the hon. member with regard to the annual report, he is confusing two kinds of reports. The report which is contemplated by clause 5 of the bill is a report by the Minister of Finance to be tabled in the house as provided. In this respect the present bill follows the Bretton Woods legislation precisely, and the Minister of Finance annually tables in this house a report on the operations of the various Bretton Woods organizations.
Some time ago in accordance with a similar clause in the Bretton Woods legislation I tabled an annual report which covered the operations of the international bank for reconstruction and development, the international monetary fund and the international finance corporation. If this bill passes it will be the responsibility of the Minister of Finance next year and each succeeding fiscal year to lay his report before parliament within 30 days after the end of that fiscal year or, if parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first 30 days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
[Mr. Regier.l

The hon. member asked about reports of these organizations themselves. These organizations do issue annual reports; at least their responsible officers do. Those reports are submitted to the annual meetings of the governors of these institutions; that is to say, the governors of the international bank, the governors of the international monetary fund and the directors of the international finance corporation. Those meetings are normally held in the last week of September or sometimes in early October, depending on where they are held. No minister of finance of this country has any control over the date when those reports are issued; they are not his reports. His report as provided by this legislation is a different document entirely.
The final matter that was raised by the hon. member concerned the details of management of some organizations engaged on an international basis in sending aid, such as the Colombo plan. The administration of the Colombo plan as far as Canada is concerned is a matter of interest principally to three departments of government; the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Finance. On the administrative side the Department of Trade and Commerce is the one principally involved, because the Colombo plan organization operates under that department. The practice when I was a private member and a member of the standing committee on external affairs of this house was that we always made our inquiries and detailed review of the operations of the Colombo plan and Canada's part in it annually on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs in the standing committee on external affairs.

I would like to say a brief word on this point which has been raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, because I think it is an important point. We urge that the treasure of this country should be shared with other countries by assisting the less developed countries of the world. Sometimes one runs into considerable opposition in putting forward what I believe most of us in this house recognize as an essential policy on the part of government in the interdependent world in which we live. But if we run into these objections, sometimes responsibly made and sometimes irresponsibly made, we should be prepared to give evidence of careful administration in the dispensation of funds which go from the Canadian taxpayer to assist people in other countries.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked how we could get reports on the operation of this particular institution* with

special emphasis on the part that Canada has committed herself to play. I should think it must be clear at the outset that the opportunity in the case of the international development association is not as easy as in the case of the Colombo plan. The assistance given by the international development association is institutional assistance. The administration of the fund in the case of the l.D.A. is something that resides outside of Canada. The operation will be through the directors, who have a close affiliation with the international bank. In fairness I think one should say that the administration of the bank under Mr. Black has been so efficient that one may be sure that the moneys appropriated by this parliament are going to be carefully expended by him and his colleagues; but in any event that does not alter the right of the hon. member to question or to ascertain what has been done with the funds voted by parliament.
The minister, of course, will have to account for any funds voted by this parliament and expended by Canada as a member of the international development association. There would be that opportunity, I suspect, not only through interrogation and debate in the house but through participation in the committees of the house and particularly in the committee on external affairs.
With regard to Colombo plan expenditures, I do not know what the hon. member had in mind particularly when referring to the reactor in Bombay. I am not questioning his right to refer to that expenditure, because the contribution of Canada was very considerable. I believe the total expenditure is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $40 million, half of which came from Canada. One would want to make sure that the moneys spent on a project like that or on any other project were wisely spent.
In the case of the Colombo plan it should be remembered that the control on the part of the donor country is much greater, at least in principle, than it would be in the case of the project immediately before us, because the Colombo plan does not operate institutionally. It may be an international association in terms of general policy, but whatever moneys are expended by an individual country are expended by that country as the result of a bilateral arrangement made with the receiving country. In that narrower relationship there is a greater opportunity of checking up on the expenditure than there would be in the case of institutional assistance. I believe the hon. member was justified in putting this question, because *we have to be able to satisfy ourselves and the Canadian people that the moneys expended in this way are being wisely spent.

In the committee on banking and commerce we were all greatly encouraged to feel that we are very fortunate in having a new fund of this kind completely in the hands of experienced people such as those who have administered the world bank.
It is a remarkable achievement on the part of those connected with the world bank to be able to report that over 13 years they have lent $5 billion without loss. I believe those loans have gone to some 50 countries around the world. The Minister of Finance is a governor of the world bank and the international monetary fund. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONTRIBUTIONS, PENSIONABLE SERVICE, BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Public Service Superannuation Act was enacted in 1953 and came into effect on January 1, 1954. This resolution contemplates a number of amendments to the act to which the government has been giving consideration for some time. The most important of the amendments are designed to improve substantially the value of the basic benefits available to most civil servants who contribute to the superannuation account. Corresponding amendments provide for adjustments to rates of contribution. Other

amendments make provision for improved benefits to smaller groups of persons, and others are designed to streamline the administration of the act.
Earlier today I tabled three reports submitted to me by the chief actuary of the Department of Insurance on the actuarial valuations of the superannuation account, the public service death benefit account and the regular services death benefit account respectively. It was necessary for the government to receive the actuarial valuations of the various accounts maintained for the purposes of this act before the nature of the amendments thereto and their actuarial implications could be determined. The last of these reports was received subsequent to the last session of parliament.
I have received many requests concerning the pensions of civil servants. A great number related to increases in the pensions of persons already retired. These matters were dealt with at the last two sessions of parliament and embodied in the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act, 1959. Many requests have been made seeking improvements in the basic benefit formula for those who have not yet retired.
The basic benefit formula applicable to most civil servants who contribute to the superannuation account provides for a pension equal to the number of years of pensionable service up to 35 years, multiplied by 2 per cent of the average salary received by the pensioner over the period of 10 consecutive years in which his salary was highest. The representations which I have received have sought a reduction in the 10-year average salary formula, and thus an enhancement of the value of benefits received.
Accordingly it is proposed to introduce amendments which will establish the formula on the basis of the best consecutive six-year average instead of the previous 10-year average. This change will place the formula applicable under the Public Service Superannuation Act on the same basis as that now available to new members of the regular forces and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under their superannuation statutes. The uniformity in the basis of benefits throughout our superannuation legislation thus achieved, and which has heretofore been lacking, will represent a major advance for civil servants and a major improvement in administration.
I should mention that the amendments to which I have just referred in no way impair the position of a diminishing number of civil servants who fell into special categories on the coming into force of the earlier civil service superannuation act on July 19, 1924
Public Service Superannuation Act and elected to contribute under that act during the following three years, thus qualifying for a pension calculated on a basis of the average salary over the last five years of service.
The Public Service Superannuation Act provides pension benefits comparing favourably with those of most private plans in Canada. It has been generally recognized in the civil service that under a plan of this nature, where costs are shared by civil servants and by the government as employer, it is only equitable that the cost of major improvements in the benefits should also be shared. Thus the improvement proposed in the benefit formula is coupled with an amendment which provides for an increase in the male contribution rate from 6 per cent to 62 per cent of salary. No increase in the female contribution rate of 5 per cent is to be made. A corresponding increase will be made in the matching contribution made by the government. Thus the over-all rate of contribution will be 13 per cent for male employees and 10 per cent for female employees.
The additional cost to the government in a full year will be an estimated $2.5 million, based on salary rates in effect as of January 1, 1960. There will be some small upward revision of this figure to take account of salary increases granted or contemplated in 1960. The change from the 10-year average to the six-year average in the basic benefit formula will increase the value of benefits available under the superannuation act by $21 million as of January 1, 1960. Again, there will be a small increase in this amount to take account of salary increases granted or contemplated in 1960.
The other proposed major change in benefits relates to the supplementary death benefit provided under part II of the act. At present this commences to decrease after age 60 and disappears entirely on retirement or at age 70, whichever is the later. An amendment will be proposed providing that every person with five years' continuous employment participating under part II of the act will on his 65th birthday, either as an employee or as a pensioner if he was entitled to an immediate annuity on retirement, be credited with a paid-up $500 death benefit as part of his over-all benefit protection.
The cost of this benefit will be borne entirely by the government. It is estimated that this change will involve an additional expenditure of about $1.5 million in the first full year and $500,000 annually thereafter, increasing with the growth in the number of participants.
Another measure which I am sure will commend itself to the committee is one

Public Service Superannuation Act which will provide for alleviation in the conditions which require a reduction of pension during short periods of re-employment in the civil service. The present formula, which calls for a reduction in the pension after as little as one day of re-employment in many cases, will be replaced by another which calls for a determination based on the salary received in each quarter by a re-employed civil service pensioner. This will eliminate the majority of the pension adjustments which otherwise would have had to be made in the future.
The bill proposes that the amendments relating to increased contributions shall come into force at a time provided for by the governor general in council. It is my intention to recommend that, after second reading, the bill be referred to a special committee where it will be possible to study the amendments and the changes in the basic benefit and contribution formulas in detail.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONTRIBUTIONS, PENSIONABLE SERVICE, BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure the committee of the whole is very much interested in this resolution and the subject of providing pensions or retirement benefits for employees of the public service. This subject is one that has occupied the House of Commons from time to time for a great many years and on many occasions.
However, I think it fair to say that the present concept of superannuation, as we understand it, had its origin in the work of the committee of 1923 which examined this whole field of civil service legislation and civil service superannuation. As a result of this very splendid piece of work done by this committee headed by Hon. James Malcolm, we had the civil service superannuation act of 1924, which I think was a considerable departure from the legislation in operation up to that time and was the basis of our present legislation.
Then in 1938 and again in 1939 there was a committee of this house set up to examine into this subject. Much excellent work was done by that committee in those years. Unfortunately the legislation which that committee recommended had to be postponed by reason of the intervention of the war in 1939 and its continuance for some years. It was not until 1944 that the amendments were made to the 1924 act, a period of 20 years having elapsed without any basic change in the legislation.
It is interesting that in the 1924 legislation there were two conditions precedent of special significance before an employee was entitled to receive superannuation on retirement. One of those conditions was that he must come under what was then called the status of a permanent employee. The word
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1
"permanent" seemed to have been given a secondary meaning in the legislation relating to the civil service at that time, and indeed until very recent times, and the word "temporary" to been given a secondary meaning that was quite different from its ordinary meaning.
In any event, the "temporaries" were excluded from the benefits of the legislation until the 1944 amendment, and all persons who were not paid on the basis of a stated annual salary were excluded from the possibility of benefits under the 1924 legislation. That provision applied to great numbers of persons. For instance, persons with trades training in the printing bureau who were paid on a weekly basis were excluded from the act because they did not meet the requirement of the legislation of being in receipt of a stated annual salary.
In 1944 a new departure was made and large numbers of temporaries or so-called temporaries and persons who were paid other than on the basis of a stated annual salary were included. Then in 1947 amendments were made improving the legislation and adopting more of the recommendations of the committee of 1938 and 1939. Then there were subsequent amendments in 1953. Prior to the 1953 bill the whole principle of the receipt of benefits had been that they were payable as a matter of grace rather than as a matter of right to the civil servant. The 1953 act changed that basis altogether and made the superannuation benefits payable as a matter of right to the employee on retiring rather than as a matter of grace. A great many other changes were made. However, the whole nature of the change was to extend what already, in relation to the times, was a good piece of legislation and a very satisfactory one in relation to the concept on this subject current at that time.
From 1953 onward there have been other consequential amendments, all of which I think were improvements in the act. They tended to meet the changing concepts on this subject and to enlarge the number of civil servants who are entitled to come under the scope of this legislation.
The resolution before us is a rather interesting one. It deals specifically with nine subject matters or nine changes. It is a resolution preceding a measure to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act on nine different points; namely, with respect to contributions, pensionable service, benefits, the calculation of annuities paid to widows and children, persons re-employed, medical examinations, transferred pensionable employees, contributions to the retirement fund, reciprocal transfer agreements and certain other changes.

A great many representations have been put forward to the minister by responsible associations of the civil service. Indeed, I think a great many of them have been circulated among all hon. members. I suppose it would be technically possible to argue the merits or demerits of each of those numerous recommendations, but I do not think that is the effective way in which to approach this legislation today. From what the minister has said I take it that while there may be a great number of subject matters covered and a great number of amendments, there is not any extensive basic new principle involved in the new legislation.
I was interested to hear the minister advise the committee that three actuarial reports have been tabled dealing with the condition of the fund. I shall look forward with interest to seeing those documents and to seeing what the situation is. I have not seen them; I am not familiar with them, so it would be useless to debate them.
I was interested to hear the minister say that the rights of those persons under the old retirement act of 1919 and 1920 are preserved and are not affected. That has been a problem of some real concern. Some of them felt they should have come under that act, particularly so far as it involved retirement benefit based on five years' employment rather than ten years. The matter has been one of some controversy and concern over the years. With the change in the main act reducing the term of service on which superannuation is based from ten years to six, the difficulty, for that reason as well as from the effluxion of time, will, of course, have largely disappeared.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us reads, in part, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act, and this is the time for us to express our opinions as to what these amendments ought to contain.
It has long been my contention that any act of this kind ought to arrange for pensions to be automatically raised or lowered as the cost of living rises or falls. 1 remember a former minister of finance announcing in this house that if he were able to accommodate pensioners in this matter he would establish for himself the reputation of being the most famous minister of finance anywhere in the world. However, he was a little in error, in that there are many ministers of finance in the western democratic world who have made arrangements whereby people on fixed incomes have those incomes moved upward or downward in step with the cost of living. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the measure which the present resolution would authorize to be introduced is of the highest importance. It touches all aspects of the appointment, classification, tenure, rights and responsibilities of the civil service of Canada, and the powers and duties of the independent civil service commission charged with responsibility in relation thereto.
The present Civil Service Act enacted in 1918 is a landmark in Canadian history. It was a major advance over all the legislation which preceded it, including the acts of 1868, 1882, 1885 and 1908. At a stroke it placed the recruitment, promotion, classification and organization of the Civil Service Act of Canada beyond the reach of partisan political interference, and laid the foundation of what has come to be known as "the merit system". For many years the Civil Service Act has been the bulwark of this principle.
This principle, however, has not withstood all the tests to which it has been submitted. During world war II overriding legislation was adopted which permitted both the principles and the provisions of the act to be ignored and practices and procedures to grow up at variance with the letter of the law. During the post-war period it became increasingly clear that strict adherence to

the provisions of the act prevented the civil service commission from giving such service to departments of government as it was required and indeed desired to give, particularly in the fields of organization and classification. In these latter fields the expansion of the country and the enlargement of the federal government's commitments posed special problems.
Since 1918 the functions of the civil service have undergone a transformation and proliferation. Its tasks have become infinitely more diverse, more complex, more technical and more specialized in keeping with the vast extension of the public business and the activities of government. More and more it has been recognized as essential to good government that Canada should maintain a public service of the highest competence in many fields and of unchallenged integrity.
At the request first of Mr. St. Laurent in 1957, then of the present government on its accession to office in June of that year, the civil service commission conducted a review of the entire field of personnel administration in the public service with a view to revision of the Civil Service Act. Its report, which has been commonly named after the then chairman of the commission, Mr. Heeney, was in due course presented to the government, and was tabled in parliament early in 1959. It has attracted the widest interest across Canada. The government has acknowledged its deep appreciation to Mr. Heeney and the two commissioners, Miss Addison and Mr. Pelletier, for this very valuable report.
The report does not in any sense purport to be a draft statute, but it contains in appendix A a detailed list of provisions which it suggests should be incorporated either in the act or in the regulations made pursuant thereto. I am informed that it was not the purpose in drawing up this appendix to use language which would be necessarily appropriate to such enactments, nor to do more than suggest the subject matters and the method of treating them as a guide to the draftsman in drawing the bill, subject always to the views of the government on matters of policy. It therefore follows that the language of the bill, taking into account the special requirements of an act of parliament, will rarely conform to that of the recommendations contained in the report. Particularly in that area of decision as to what should properly be contained in the body of the bill and what should be assigned to regulations to be made pursuant to it, it has been necessary to modify the commission's suggestions.
It should be noted also that the report contemplates the eventual establishment of a
Civil Service Act
single civil service which would embrace the employees of a number of agencies which have been established by separate acts of parliament with provisions which are peculiar to the agencies themselves and under which they have been working for many years. The government does not at this time propose to disturb the composition of the civil service by adding to it the personnel of agencies not subject to the existing act. Such a course would involve the submission to parliament of amendments to the numerous statutes which constitute such agencies now and the wholesale incorporation within the civil service of large numbers of men and women without consultation and without sufficient examination of the problems which such a step would entail.
The report proposed that the commission should give up its responsibility for approving the organization of government departments and, while retaining an advisory function in this field, in which it has become expert over the years, permit deputy heads of departments to be masters in their own houses where questions of departmental organization are concerned, subject to the approval and authority of the governor in council. It was further proposed in the report that more flexibility in matters of recruitment and selection of personnel for the civil service be permitted to the commission and, let me say at once, only to the commission, under circumstances which might in its opinion render the usual procedure by way of competition impracticable and unsuitable, and where the commission might deem it desirable to delegate these functions in special circumstances to deputy heads. These two cardinal recommendations of the commissioners have been adopted and incorporated in the bill.
The bill reaffirms and establishes the principles of the merit system as exemplified in provisions for selection and classification of employees in the civil service of Canada by a strong and independent civil service commission and by that commission alone. Anything less would be a renunciation of a tradition of which this country may well be proud, the tradition of the independence of our civil service which has placed it in the front rank of similar organizations throughout the world.
The bill also contains a definition of the public service extending beyond the civil service itself. This definition will extend to employees of agencies outside the civil service but within the greater compass of the public service the privilege of transfer and promotion into the civil service on the same basis as employees who are already in the civil service.

Civil Service Act
The present act contains no provision for the right of appeal by an employee to the civil service commission, although the regulations made pursuant to it provide for such appeals as are now taken. The bill will contain explicit provision for the composition of appeal boards under the authority of the commission and for the circumstances under which an appeal may be taken, including the right of appeal against a departmental recommendation to dismiss an employee.
In keeping with the spirit of the times, recognition is given to two important principles which have engaged the attention of staff associations within the civil service; first, that the pay of an employee is a matter not of grace but right, and second, that consultation between the staff associations and appropriate officers of the government or the commission on questions of pay and conditions of work as the need arises is desirable. These principles are either expressly recommended or implied in the Heeney report.
The present statute provides for an employee appointed to a local position to be qualified in the knowledge and use of the language of the majority of persons with whom he is required to do business, be it French or English. The proposed bill, however, recognizes additionally the desirability of giving a preference not only to those who can speak the language of the majority but to those who are skilled in the use of both the official languages of this country, not only when appointed to local positions but also to positions at the main offices of departments wherever, in the opinion of the civil service commission, effective service requires them to be placed.
The government does not think it right at this time to give effect to those recommendations in the report which would have the effect of altering the existing law providing for preference in competitions for entry into the service in the case of veterans of the first and second world wars and the campaign in Korea. The law which was established in this respect by the previous administration may not have proved uniformly satisfactory in all its aspects, but it represents a covenant between the nation and its returned servicemen the terms of which cannot be enlarged or abridged at this late date without injury to both parties. If the entitlement were now enlarged to confer the preference upon those who did not possess it heretofore, all those servicemen who were applicants for vacancies in the civil service over these past years and who have not enjoyed its benefits would feel unjustly treated in retrospect. If it were in any way limited or curtailed by restricting,

for instance, its application to only one occasion, such action would constitute a breach of faith which the government declines to contemplate.
The house will therefore observe, when the bill is examined, that the veterans preference provisions of the present act are maintained intact subject to a direct reference to the situation of veterans of the Korean campaign as contained in the Veterans Benefit Act.
Generally speaking, therefore, the bill contains the best of the existing legislation, provides for the removal of such anomalies as have arisen in the course of the application of the former during over 40 years, and plainly provides for either the authorization or prohibition of many of the practices which have grown up without sanction during this period.
The bill is somewhat longer than the present act. The government recognizes the need for careful examination of it by parliament. To facilitate such detailed consideration I shall propose that the bill, following second reading, be referred to a special select committee of the house for study and report. I think it is obvious that our resolution procedure is not well adapted-

As a matter of fact, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) stated this:
We have not yet managed to curb the chaps at the civil service commission, but we will do it yet and then we are the ones who will be running all that business.

As I said, I wish to make only a few comments on that to indicate the feeling of the civil servants across this nation who have sent these letters to many, many people. It is a key point of bargaining rights that I am leading up to. I do not think anything else, regardless of whether it is a benevolent attitude at election time or at any other time to establish upward adjustments or otherwise in civil servants' salaries, will meet the point. The main point is that here are many thousands of people in the public service of Canada who do not have the rights that are enjoyed by countless thousands of other people across this nation, namely the human and civil right to make a determination of, or participate in making a determination of their own, in consultation and discussion with their employer, a determination of what their working conditions, wages and other provisions relating to their work will be.
As the committee knows, I introduced a bill earlier this session in this regard. There was some discussion of it. I do not intend to go into it. It was a bill to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. It was designed to make that act, with some exceptions, applicable to the public service of Canada. It met with a number of objections. What I should like to do is to lay the groundwork here to indicate what I think should be included in the bill when it is presented to the house. These objections revolve mainly around the fact that in the final analysis parliament should have the right to determine what the salary structure will be and what wages will be paid to civil servants, since parliament has the right to decide in the final analysis what all other payments out of the public treasury will be. Perhaps there should be a modification of the original thoughts that I had on this matter to meet this point. I think that a conciliation board or an arbitration board, or whatever you wish to call it, should be established, although in the strict sense of the word it

would not be an arbitration board that I intend to suggest but a conciliation board of the public service of Canada.
I think the public service should have the right to proceed to such a board if it cannot find satisfaction in its contract negotiations and at other stages. I think that a report of this board should be tabled in parliament and that parliament itself should make the final recommendation so that parliament would then have the final say as to what rates would be applied to the public service rather than have the minister in his ivory tower decide what those rates would be.
As I said earlier, he is now doing that in an arbitrary and discriminatory way. There is some reference also in the initial Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to the fact that perhaps the definition section there of employee is not strictly applicable to the public service because certainly the structure of the public service is not strictly comparable with any private industry and perhaps there should be some modification there.
With these two modifications that I have suggested and the one that I initially proposed, namely that there should not be the right to strike, we think the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, if the government so desired, could be properly embodied within the Civil Service Act, to set up the machinery whereby the civil servants could reach fair and just settlement and equity in their dealings with the government, not only with respect to wages and salary adjustments, but also with respect to the resolution of disputes and differences of opinion between the time when they are actually bargaining for an alteration in any collective agreement that they may have and other times. This relates to such things as classifications of employees, promotions and allocations within different departments, rates of pay and whether they are receiving a fair rate of pay for the particular type of work they are doing, and all of these other matters which will arise from time to time in any organization. When a person feels he is aggrieved and has a grievance he should have the right to proceed in this instance to the board of arbitration to determine whether or not he is right in his suggestion that he has been aggrieved.
I think, Mr. Chairman, this is the key point to which we should direct ourselves. I refer to the giving of bargaining rights to civil servants, to the people in the public service, to determine, as all other employees in industry have, their own destiny to a degree; the right to form themselves into organizations, to bargain collectively with

their employer. This is the basic human right that we think should be embodied in the Prime Minister's bill of rights if and when we get around to seeing it. But this is one of the rights that I think individuals within the public service should have just the same as people in private industry have. Without this right, without providing the machinery by which a member of the public service of Canada may state his objections, without the right to a piece of machinery through which he can express himself, and collaborate with others in a similar class of work, and attempt to deal with his employer; without those rights placed in the Civil Service Act we shall continue to have the recurrence, maybe not year after year but time after time as the years go on of the attitude that is existing at the moment among many of the people in our civil service.
The attitude expressed in the form letter I read earlier also expressed my views, and I say it is not good for our public servants to have this sort of attitude toward the government. It is not good to have a policy toward the public service that continually makes for dissatisfaction and causes some employees to leave the civil service and seek other fields of employment because there is a better opportunity for the expression of themselves as individuals in private industry. We should not allow a situation to continue which creates such hard feeling.

If the minister would do something of that nature I think he would do a great deal to dispel the frustration and anger existing among our civil servants at the present time and help greatly to prevent a recurrence in the future.

Among the factors is one concerning the cost of living and another concerning the supplementary cost of living. The method of arriving at the cost of living and the supplementary cost of living allowance is one which in my view is producing certain inequitable results so far as the actual rates are concerned.
The previous government set up a committee known as the interdepartmental committee on isolated post regulations, and the recommendations of that committee are either accepted or rejected by treasury board in arriving at the rate of allowance to be paid to the northern civil servant. In arriving at an assessment of the factors in order that a rate of allowance may be calculated the committee has recourse to information provided on certain forms which are supposed to be completed by civil servants in the north. In the past these forms have been poorly distributed and have not been fully completed. As a result erroneous information has come to the hands of the administration both prior to the time that present government took office and subsequent thereto.
I suggest that a more accurate method of assessing the factors which are properly considered when arriving at the rate of allowance to be paid would be to conduct an on the spot survey of conditions in the post which is being assessed. The cost of living allowance, of course, has to do with the cost of food in these remote areas, and the supplementary cost of living allowance has to do with the cost of other goods and services supplied in the area which may be under examination. Recently there has been a reduction in both these allowances on the recommendation of the interdepartmental committee on isolated post allowances, a committee which incidentally, is composed entirely of civil servants. In effect, therefore, it is a recommendation made by civil servants for a reduction in the isolated post allowance of civil servants.
I think the information the committee had on which it based its recommendation for this reduction was far from complete. As a result, I feel that a more accurate assessment should be made and in the meantime any positive action with relation to a reduction of these allowances should continue to be suspended. For instance, at the moment the method of calculating the cost of living allowance is

Civil Service Act
by determining the relative difference between the cost of food in Vancouver or Edmonton and that in the given location in the north. I feel that the calculation of the allowance by relying on the relative difference is wrong. What should be done is to conduct an on the spot survey of the cost of food in any given location and upon that basis the rate of allowance should be arrived at.
As to the supplementary cost of living allowance, the cost of other goods and services in the remoter northern areas should be assessed and likewise calculated. This is now calculated simply by an arbitrary guess as to what the allowance should be. The method which I suggest should be adopted is an on the spot survey of the actual cost of other goods and services in these various locations. If this method is substituted in each case for the method employed by the previous administration and still carried on by the present administration, perhaps because the matter has not been brought to the minister's attention before, I think a much more accurate assessment of such allowances could be made. With these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, may I say it is my hope that there will be some provision in the new act or the regulations that will be made thereunder which will result in a revision of the method of calculating these allowances so that a much more accurate and equitable allowance may be paid.

A technical argument could probably be made that the principle of the merit system was attempted to be introduced in earlier legislation, but in any event the 1918 act certainly was a landmark on this subject and was properly described by the minister as such. Newton Wesley Rowell, afterwards chief justice of Ontario, for the contribution they made in that regard. It seems to me that in their remarks they showed an appreciation of the problem and suggested methods whereby real strength could be achieved in the administrative arm of government which have served as a good base on which to operate.
