I do not know what is reversed about it. The minister of finance introduced the legislation in that time because apparently at that time the secretary of state did not have so much to do with the legislation. In the last number of years it has been the responsibility of the secretary of state and I, for one, am thoroughly mystified as to why the Secretary of State is not presenting this legislation today.
Be that as it may, when I started my remarks I was mentioning the importance of principles laid down by former leaders. There is a particularly good reference from the leader of the union government, when he spoke about the civil service being free from the maligning influence of patronage. The whole attempt has been to get away from that patronage and establish a truly merit system of appointment. I, therefore, welcome a review of this legislation at this stage to see what improvement can be made.
It is rather interesting that the1 last government, when the new chairman of the civil service commission, Mr. Heeney, was appointed, directed him to deal with this subject, to examine the whole subject and to make a report and recommendations. The new government when it came in renewed that direction in very similar terms. Clearly, Mr. Chairman, I take it there was no difference in the reference intended, so we have the Heeney report to which the Minister of Finance, in introducing this measure, made so much reference. There is a particularly good paper dealing with the subject of the Heeney report by one of the commissioners of the civil service commission, Mr. Paul Pelletier, on October 23, 1959. This will be found in the proceedings of the 11th annual conference of the institute of public administration of Canada. There is an abundance of good material on this subject and, quite frankly, in discussing a subject which is so wide there is some difficulty in knowing just which segment should be discussed.
I wanted to raise one more matter, and I think in order to do so I should quote a line or two from the Heeney report. This will be found on page 8 of that report, paragraph No. 17. It reads:
Law alone cannot guarantee good administration, but it can and does have a real effect on the quality of the personnel who are recruited and it can provide incentives to good performance.
There is more said about the subject, and then the report goes on to say this:
The effectiveness of the present act in protecting the national service from these traditional abuses-

Referring to the abuse of patronage and other abuses.
-is a convincing argument for the preservation of the essential legal safeguards of the merit principle.
The minister indicated he was attempting to preserve and strengthen that principle in the legislation he is seeking to introduce. I feel that that paragraph makes it clear that there are two principles that are involved in developing a healthy and strong civil service. One is the legislation itself, and that has been relatively good legislation in this country and we hope the new bill will be a good bill when it comes before us, and the other thing is the attitude of the government itself toward its own administrative arm.
I am bound to admit that as I studied the history of Canada I have observed over the years, differing attitudes by different governments to the administrative arm of government. There have been periods when, unfortunately, the treatment of the civil service was not such as most of us in this house would wish. Since the recent change in government I have, at times, been somewhat concerned with the attitude of this government toward the civil service. The Minister of Finance, I am quite sure, as time goes on and his experience continues will come to the conclusion that his method of handling the pay increases over the last year-quite in addition to the question of the pay increases themselves, the amounts and so on-leaves something to be desired. It seems to me that it does not reveal on the part of the government an appreciation of the proper place of the civil service in the functioning of government in Canada. I could labour that subject for some time, but I hope the minister will pay more attention to that subject in the future so that we will not have the same rather peremptory announcements such as were made during the last year. I must say, frankly, that I had regarded the Civil Service Act as doing one outstanding thing and that was setting up a commission that was answerable to parliament.
There are quite adequate safeguards in that, such as the provision that the chairman of the civil service commission can only be removed by a joint address of the two houses of parliament, which is the method of removal that is made applicable to judges of the supreme court. Here we can see the lengths to which our predecessors went in seeking to guarantee the independence of the civil service commission from partisan interference by government. I do not want to reiterate a debate that took place earlier as I am not 79951-0-325
Civil Service Act
sure of the extent to which I could do it, although I believe I could bring it under the rules.
I must say I was shocked with an answer given by the Minister of Finance when he was asked to table a report of the commission to the government. Possibly the nature of his answer was dictated by the procedure on motions for the production of papers which would not permit the minister to debate the matter. Perhaps I should be charitable to the minister as certainly the answer was in an abbreviated form, and the form in which it appeared on that occasion was such as to weaken the confidence of the public service of Canada in the government's attitude toward that service.
I could pick out other points, but perhaps I have said enough to indicate that I am very concerned that this legislation being introduced shall in no way weaken that principle of the independence of the commission from the partisan influence of the government of the day. This principle should be preserved and strengthened.
There is another point that concerns me greatly. The last really thorough study of the civil service was in 1938 and 1939. I was interested in noting, when I sent for the evidence of this committee, that the special committee of 1938 held some 48 sittings. The committee was reconvened in 1939 and held nine meetings. In other words, on that occasion some 57 meetings were held on the Civil Service Act. This leads me to say that in my opinion no government of Canada can be really effective in the interests of the public of this country without a strong and competent civil service, a civil service with a high morale and efficiency. I believe we have such a service, and I believe it is important that we always have such a service.
We are told by the minister that the legislation now coming before us is going to be longer than is the present act. The present act has some 65 sections to it. It is divided into five parts, one part which, by the way, seems to deal with the subject of compensation. I will not elaborate too much on that matter. However, to deal with that act and to review it required some 57 meetings of a special committee the last time it was done. We are now going to be asked to review the whole subject matter and to consider a new act that is longer than this one of 65 sections and to do it all, as the minister said, "I hope rather hurriedly" this session without having the opportunity to think about them.
I am going to make a direct appeal to the minister to consider this whole matter in order to ascertain if the interest of the country would not be better served by allowing this bill, once it is introduced and is

Civil Service Act
given first reading, to stand over so that a committee can be set up at the start of a session, one that can look forward with interest and eagerness to holding 57 sittings or more, if necessary, in order to deal with this matter thoroughly and to give it the kind of treatment it deserves.
I have had some opportunity of dealing with civil service associations, civil service bodies and civil servants individually and I think I can assure any committee to be set up that some numbers of civil service associations will wish to be heard. I think it is appropriate and proper that they should be heard. The act, the regulations thereunder and the procedures are quite cumbrous and quite involved. They are not simple things that can be dealt with in a few minutes. I would hope that all these organizations would feel that they are going to have the opportunity of being heard, of making full representations and of submitting to examination by members of the committee so that the bill as it is finally enacted by the house will be one that will meet all the requirements of good government, that will have been examined thoroughly and that the civil service-whose charter it will be, in reality- will feel that it has been competently examined by the house and by the committee.
I therefore repeat with all the strength at my command the request to the minister to reconsider this matter, that he let the bill, after first reading, stand over and have the committee set up immediately after the throne speech so that the months required for full examination of the bill may be available.
There are many subjects, briefs and sections that will require to be examined. Any lesser treatment of the matter is not one that will serve the interests of the country or of the government adequately and well. I perhaps have no need to draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that this is the 106th day of the session. According to my arithmetic, if the committee were to hold the same number of meetings as the former committee held, it would be the 163rd day of the session, if the committee held a sitting every day from now on for the rest of this session, before it could even start to prepare its report. From this calculation hon. members will see just how serious this matter is and I hope they will join me in the request I am making to the minister.
A good deal could be said about governments of the day. It seems to me that the situation is this, as I have been able to study it. If you examine governments since confederation, Mr. Chairman, you will find a rather interesting coincidence, namely that

governments which have been incompetent, if I may use that word, or which have been antagonistic in their handling of this subject or which have misunderstood the role of the civil servant in the art of government or in the business of government have tended to be weak governments and have tended to destroy themselves. It is a rather interesting study for anyone to pursue. While I cannot express too many wishes for the present government, I would hope they would not fall into the error of treating this subject in any way less seriously than its inherent merit demands.
There is a great range of subjects requiring discussion. I noted that the minister indicated he is changing the provisions having to do with the pay of an employee of the crown being a matter of right instead of a matter of grace, following a principle that was laid down in the civil service superannuation legislation some years ago. Then he mentions that consultation between the staff associations and the appropriate officers of the government or the commission on questions of pay and conditions of work as the need arises is desirable. There is a whole area of discussion there. I do not propose to spend the rest of the time allotted to me this afternoon in discussing it. But because of its complexity, that subject alone deserves close attention from all hon. members. I am not sure just what the minister meant in that reference or just what he proposes in the legislation. We look forward with interest to seeing what the legislation contains on that subject. With the growth of the service and with the changing ideas of our times it is readily apparent that the present method of consultation is not working efficiently and is not adequate as in regard to the present needs.
I must revert to an earlier point. I place a little bit of blame for that situation on the minister's attitude or, shall I say, his failure to understand the whole subject and his failure to give to the workers in the service the confidence which they deserve and to which they are entitled as long as they are doing their work efficiently and in the interests of the country.
Then there is this other matter mentioned by the minister, namely the changing situation to be covered by legislation, the matter of the veteran preferences in relation to such things as the war in Korea which did not involve the kind of declaration of war envisaged by the earlier legislation and matters of that kind. We could go on then into this whole question of existing legislation, the method of the rates of pay, the rates of compensation for new classes; the method of

submitting the reports for the rates of compensation; to whom are they to be submitted; what is the method of handling them after they are submitted; what is the method of having them made public; what is the method of having them made available to parliament and so on. I think that whole sector of the act needs strengthening and needs to be brought up to date. On that point I await with interest the provisions of the bill.
Again I do not want to revert to something already dealt with, but I must say I was rather shocked at what I thought was the limitation the minister was seeking to put on the debate. That is past now, but the whole matter not only of rates of pay but of methods of determining and examining them to see that they are adequate, and so on, requires minute consideration by some appropriate procedure of parliament, which in this case I would say is the special committee. Then there are all the other matters to be considered, such as the development of the Whitley councils as they were first created in the United Kingdom a number of years ago and their adaptation to this country, the modernization of them to meet modern needs, the extent to which they should be adopted, modernized and improved, and the extent to which they should be discontinued because they may not be quite up to date. All that covers a vast area.
It is not my purpose to develop the argument any further at this stage. I for one want to see this bill. I hope it will be possible, when the bill is made available to me, to have a proper opportunity of reading and studying it thoroughly and that I will not be expected to deal with it in a rush at the committee stage when we have such important committees sitting as the committee dealing with the combines legislation, the committee dealing with broadcasting and the committee dealing with the bill of rights.
Therefore I conclude my remarks with the reiteration of my request to the minister to lay before his colleagues consideration of procedure from here on in the handling of this piece of legislation. As I said, when the act was previously before the special committee in 1938 and 1939 it required some 57 sittings to deal with it. We are now in our 106th day of this session, and if we are expected to deal with this legislation in a special committee, bring it back to the house and enact the legislation at this session, I am afraid it will get less competent treatment from us than it deserves, and less competent treatment than any one of us would wish it to get. It will also create a situation in the civil service where there will be further demoralization.

I do not think the government's method of handling the increases has been quite up to what it should have been. As I say, I do not propose to state a case. For instance, discussing the question of the failure to make these increases retroactive to the appropriate date, not following the earlier practice in this regard, would occupy me for some time. I could discuss the whole question of failure to deal with what is probably one of the most underpaid classes in the civil service, namely the postal employees. Any suggestion on the part of hon. members that those problems have not caused concern in the civil service is, in my view, not a conscientious and complete picture of the subject at all, and I say it has not been treated in the way it should have been treated.
However, I have made my plea to the minister. I regret there is only one of his colleagues in the chamber at the moment. I do hope that the request I have made gets to his colleagues in the government and that they do consider the matter in the way in which it is put forward in an effort to make sure that this legislation which is being introduced will be the best possible legislation that the house can produce.

Mr. Chairman, two or three very definite impressions have arisen from this debate, and may I be permitted a few moments to give my thoughts with respect to them. These impressions arise from the very lengthy and rather tedious remarks of the hon. member for Hull and the hon. member for Skeena to the effect that the gentlemen to my immediate right are the only members of this committee who are interested in

Civil Service Act
the Canadian civil service. Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that those of us on this side of the house share with them a deep concern with respect to their futures and that we are determined, as they were some years ago, when they had the opportunity, to do everything possible to safeguard their interests.
There is a factor which has not been mentioned today, and I say this with all due respect to every civil servant in Canada. Much has been said today with respect to the transition of the civil servant to private business, the breaking down, it is alleged, of our civil service organization. The civil servant enjoys something that no other worker in Canada enjoys, and that is a very large measure of security. While there may be times in the course of his active life when he feels he has not been entirely fairly dealt with, he always knows that except for cause he cannot be removed from his office. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that that is an advantage that should be given some consideration in any discussion of this great working force. I can think of many other groups who have no security; I am not too far from one at the moment. Other groups also could claim they are underpaid. Some members of this group close to me make that claim. I am not among them, but I do feel that there are factors involved in employment in the government service which have not been given the credit to which they are entitled.
Mention has been made of patronage. I am very happy to say as a private member of this government it has been impossible for me to indulge in any patronage. First of all it is not my wish to seek it; second, I could not get my brother, if I had one, appointed as a janitor if there was such a job open. The civil service commission in Canada is doing a most excellent job with respect to the filling of positions. There have been some disappointments of course with respect to appointments which have been made, but by and large I am very happy to say that in my opinion the replenishing of the ranks of our civil service is entirely removed from politics.
So I say that when this resolution is adopted and the bill comes before us it will be the concern of all of us regardless of political party to analyse it from the point of view of the greatest advantage for the greatest number. I am sure the Minister of Finance as he pilots the bill through the house will demonstrate to all civil servants his sincere interest in their welfare.

subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after listening to the speech of the Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon I am wondering

if as a whole the committee takes seriously enough the question which is before it. This is not just another act that will from time to time be amended or overhauled. This is the act which affects the working conditions and status of what is the most important permanent administrative arm of the government of this country. It is often said that we have the finest civil service in the world, a great organization, outstanding people. That is all very well. We must ensure that the act governing how they are appointed, the conditions under which they will work, the basis on which they are remunerated, the method by which they will achieve promotions, the regulations concerning their tenure of office, et cetera, is also the finest act of its kind in the world.
This is not a political matter. This subject should be taken out of politics altogether. Up to a point I do not think there is too much cause for complaining that too strong a political element has been injected into the debate this afternoon. However, I feel that if I were to do justice to the importance of the subject before us I and every other hon. member in this chamber who is interested in this measure would speak for at least 40 minutes because the subject is much larger and of greater importance than one would be led to believe by what has been said in the debate today.
Parliament has had no opportunity since 1938 or 1939 to discuss the whole question of the civil service. Last year we had a small review in a committee of the house. The meetings were very friendly. The hon. member for Carleton was in attendance. We were also honoured to have the acting chief commissioner, Mr. Pelletier, present, as well as others who gave us information on conditions in the civil service and the operations of the commission. But that was not the type of study a committee of this house should have given to so broad a subject. There are many serious matters to be considered including the question of the first examination appointment. That is a great question. Promotions is another. There are also the questions of assignment, transfer, tenure of office, removal, et cetera.
Another big question that must be solved is that of consultation or collective bargaining as it is referred to by some. Hon. members do not even know what is in the bill. Perhaps some hon. members on the government side know what is in the proposed bill but certainly I do not. What is more important, those who are affected do not know what is going to be in the bill.
Surely whatever our views on the matter may be we need the assistance of those who

will be affected by this legislation. The civil service associations should have an ample opportunity to appear before the committee. The officers of the commission should also appear. Surely we will not pass a bill without giving ample opportunity to those who want to speak on various aspects of it to present their case before the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, no resolution of more basic long range significance has been or will be considered at this session of parliament than this proposal to amend, revise and consolidate the Civil Service Act. However sound may be the other legislation of this parliament, however competent the ministerial direction, all will be found wanting if the subsequent and consequent administrative responsibilities are not fulfilled by a competent, responsible and loyal public service. Everything this parliament does, everything the ministry seeks to achieve, ultimately must be enforced or carried out by public servants of all levels and grades. And so I submit that this particular legislation is basic, is of vital, fundamental and lasting significance.
I therefore deeply regretted the attitude of the hon. member for Hull. Presumably this afternoon the hon. gentleman was spokesman for the official opposition in this important matter. Did he approach this resolution in an objective way? No, the hon. gentleman engaged in a political harangue. The hon. gentleman endeavoured to drag the civil service into politics, to make the act a partisan and political issue. Nothing could be more harmful to parliament or more harmful to the civil service. I say that the hon. gentleman's remarks this afternoon were both cheap and unfair. They were totally without dignity or an understanding of the fundamental precept that the civil service must be above and beyond politics.
May I remind the hon. member for Hull and indeed also remind the hon. member for Ottawa West that it is to a very great Canadian, Sir Robert Borden, and his colleagues that Canada owes the present structure of its civil service. The monument of a civil service appointed on the merit principle, promoted on the same basis, freed from partisanship, the spoils system, the favouritism and the nepotism which plagued our earlier days, is a monument to Sir Robert Borden more lasting than the bronze and granite we observe on parliament hill.
The Heeney report of December, 1958 had this to say of the Borden bill of 1918, the bill of 40 years earlier:
It has been, said that the Civil Service Act of 1918 gave Canada, in a single step, as advanced a measure of public service reform as existed anywhere in the world.
So for more than 40 years the principles of the Borden bill have stood the test of time. To all governments, to all parties, credit is due and let credit be given. Let us keep this resolution, let us keep our discussion of it above and beyond partisanship in this chamber.

Civil Service Act
During those 42 years Canada has emerged from colony into nationhood, and the status of its civil service has kept pace with that. Without reservation I submit to the committee that our senior civil servants can hold their own at international meetings, at learned societies and in the performance of their day to day duties with the public servants of any other nation; and this submission, indeed I call it this confident assertion, I would apply to all in less senior roles. That fact itself is a vindication of the Borden Civil Service Act, in principle not amended in 42 years.

I would like to say to the hon. gentleman that during 42 years I believe on the part of governments generally there has been adherence to that sound principle and there has been in the last three years an adherence to that principle the like of which has not existed in the 22 years previous thereto.
The fact that there has been that adherence would indicate that the modernization of the act, its streamlining, if you like, its up to dating, ought to be in general conformity with those principles which have stood the test of time in Canada's rush from a frontier colony to a nation capable of foremost leadership in the world.
Though Canadians are proud of the standards of our civil service-and have reason, as I have said, to be-that fact must not lead us to smug self-satisfaction or into complacency with the status quo. By parliament and by the civil service itself there must be a constant striving for improvement in the standards of our administration of public service matters. But what I emphasize is this. Parliament must be certain at all times to preserve the great traditions of our civil service. I submit that the legislation which is introduced must be tested on that basis. For those reasons I believe the house and the country will welcome what the Minister of Finance has said in introducing this legislation this afternoon and the assurances which he has given.
The first and the most significant assurance is that the merit principle will be preserved inviolate in the proposed bill. It is the
[Mr. Bell (Carleton) .1
cornerstone on which we build. The Heeney report had this to say at page 23:
It can, we believe, be asserted with confidence that the merit system is a permanent feature of the Canadian philosophy and machinery of government.
Last year, after its detailed review of the civil service commission, the standing committee on estimates ended its report with this uncompromising declaration of the faith of the members of this house, and I quote from Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, July 2, 1959, at page 648:
In reviewing the evidence and the recommendations contained in the foregoing your committee wishes to impress upon parliament the importance and the necessity for reaffirming our belief in the fundamental and underlying principle of the public service of Canada. The principle to which we refer is generally described as the "merit system" which we suggest provides the one assurance that the civil servant wifi remain free from political or other influences in discharging his responsibility to the Canadian public.
This declaration, drafted by the hon. mem ber for Calgary South, but approved unanimously by all members of the committee representing all parties in this house, is a fulfilment of the pledge which was made to the civil service association of Canada by the Prime Minister on May 1, 1958, in what I may describe as a very sympathetic and certainly a very enlightened speech on the subject of the civil service. I quote:
Our revised Civil Service Act, I am sure, will preserve the vital principles of the merit system which have been in our legislation for the past half century. Nowadays we take it for granted that civil servants are appointed and promoted on the basis of ability. We must not forget, however, that this depends upon having the right principles in our law and the effective application of them by an impartial tribunal. This we must preserve.
The public service is so important and its work affects all Canadians so directly, that we need the best men and women in it that we can secure. That is the positive aspect of the merit system- to ensure the selection of those who will do the best job.
So there is embedded in this bill, and for all time it must be a part of Canadian theories of government, the assurance of the practice, the genuine practice of-not just lip service to [DOT]-the merit system. But let us not believe that just the mere assertion of adherence to the merit system is assurance of its practice. Here, as in so many aspects of life, eternal vigilance is the price of adherence to principle. Safeguards against internal abuses, against tailor-made competitions, against favouritism by senior officials, all these are required for the genuine practice of merit in promotions. The Heeney report, at page 8, put it this way and this is a statement always to be kept before us:
Forty years ago, and this is all too frequently forgotten, the need was also for a public service

free from nepotism, the coddling of incompetent favourites, the granting of promotions for consideration and similar internal abuses. Not much is gained if the "malign influence" of political patronage is replaced by bureaucratic patronage, which may be less apparent but which can be no less insidious and demoralizing.
Most emphatically do I agree that bureaucratic patronage is insidious and demoralizing and the new act and its administration must endeavour to eliminate bureaucratic patronage as fully and completely as political patronage. Had I to choose between them, I would support political patronage ahead of bureaucratic patronage, for the politician at least is accountable for his actions. Fortunately that choice is not necessary.
And so, basically, the merit system means simply that appointments and promotions are made on the basis of an objective determination of the relative merit of qualified candidates, under which all qualified persons have the opportunity for consideration for appointments and promotions and under which duties performed are equitably compensated.
I believe it is a major responsibility of this parliament to make civil service employment an attractive and rewarding career for any young Canadian. We need to recruit the very best of our young Canadians for government, government at all levels, not those whose prime interest is in security. To do that, the rewards additional to security must be genuine. Service of the state must be considered the very highest type of service and those who pursue such a career must be given the confidence that they will not be shot down blind alleys, will not have their potential for advancement restricted by red tape, will not have their initiative blighted by needless frustrating administrative techniques, will not have their leadership qualities lost in the giant mechanism of an inhumane bureaucracy.
For that reason, personally I welcome the assurances of the Minister of Finance that the new legislation will provide greater flexibility, greater simplicity in meeting the administrative functions of the departments of government, all without prejudice to the merit system. As I understand it, the proposed legislation will provide for a clearer division of authority. It will preserve unimpaired the authority and responsibility of the civil service commission in all matters dealing with recruitment and promotion. On the other hand, in all matters of managerial concern, greater authority for decision and action will be vested in deputy heads.
I think that is good. It is in strict conformity with the Heeney report and with what I believe are recognized as the best
Civil Service Act
principles of modern public administration. What I hope this may be able to achieve is what I might describe as a better internal relativity, that is to say, an improvement in the relationship between various classes of work and rates of pay within the civil service. What we must seek to achieve, and what I believe and hope this legislation will achieve, is the establishment of definite principles of class comparability, a reduction in the number of classifications and the removal generally of discriminations and frustrations, of blind alleys for some employees. This I believe can be accomplished and will be promoted by the principles which have been outlined to the committee this afternoon by the Minister of Finance.
I think the house will have welcomed as well the assurance of the Minister of Finance that there will be no alteration in the independent status of the civil service commission as a quasi-judicial tribunal. This is in accord with the positive assurance given by the Prime Minister to the civil service association of Canada in what I have already described as a powerful speech on May 1, 1958, a speech which, as I have said, revealed a deep understanding of and sympathy for civil service traditions. At that time the Prime Minister said:
The commission is not an arm of the government to which ministers can give direction. It derives its powers and basic instructions from parliament.
That position is fundamental to the preservation of sound principles of recruitment and promotion. Welcome indeed to the whole house, I am sure, was the appointment as chairman of the civil service commission of a man of such distinction as Mr. Justice Hughes. I think he is to be congratulated upon his willingness to leave the security of the supreme court bench, a role which he achieved at a comparatively youthful age, for a term appointment in a difficult and perplexing administrative task. As a friend of his of some 30 years now, may I say I believe the commission is fortunate indeed to have as its chief a man of such civilized mind, such keen perceptions, such articulate capacities and such basic common sense and, as well, one who all his life has been guided by a firm determination to fight for the principles in which he believes.
The minister has indicated that the bill will provide the technique for an ever-increasing participation of employees and their associations in the processes leading to a determination of conditions of employment. That is good. But this I do want to say. Responsibility is a concomitant of authority. Staff associations must display genuine responsibility, moderation in language and

Civil Service Act
statesmanship in conduct to ensure an approach to effective participation in bargaining techniques. Abusive language, extravagance of expression and action have no place in civil service negotiations and only succeed in retarding what genuine friends of the civil service seek to achieve.
On other occasions I have spoken in the house about the accomplishments of the present government in civil service matters. Let it never be forgotten that the change of government in 1957 was accomplished with the least upset to the civil service of any change in history. This government has never had enough credit for that fact, for the fact that there were virtually no dismissals, no parade of dismissed employees of the type invariably experienced after previous changes of government. From the very outset this government has not given lip service but genuine adherence to the true principles of the merit system and it is time that credit was given for that fact.
In all its actions the government has demonstrated a sympathetic, understanding approach to civil service problems. Examples are the establishment of the pay research bureau, a matter frequently proposed to the former government but invariably declined; the institution of increases for superannuated civil servants, again a matter for years, sought by them but invariably refused by the St. Laurent government; the institution of a modem medical-surgical plan; the appointment of a justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario as chairman of the civil service commission; the appointment on every practical occasion of deputy ministers from within the service; the institution of a system of class by class increases in salaries with regular and periodic reviews based on the principle of fair comparison. These are but a few of the indications of the genuine understanding of the Prime Minister and his colleagues of civil service administration and problems. This legislation is further evidence of the good faith of the government.
Therefore, pleased am I that the government has decided to send this legislation to a special committee. There in the exchange of opinion, in the clash of what I hope will be non-partisan views, I believe we can bring to relative perfection a bill which for the next 40 years will shine as a beacon of sound, progressive civil service policy as the Borden Civil Service Act has shone for the past four decades.

extravagance of words. The hon. member also boasted about the fact that the present government has not indulged in the time-honoured practice of mass dismissals since they came to office. If we look back over the last three years I think we will find they have devised a much better method, that of making things so miserable and unpleasant for people that in the end they resign.
When the minister introduced the resolution today he made reference to the Civil Service Act of 1918 as a landmark. From the extent and scope of the amendments now proposed
I	think the minister will agree that the landmark has become rather moss grown over the period of 40 odd years, and we certainly agree that it is time for a thorough overhauling of the act. The minister also made a great point about how the civil service commission has been free from political control. I wish I could be as sure as the minister that that has been the case. I am sure that many people in the civil service do not agree fully with the minister's remarks.
We must remember that the civil service commission or the Canadian government, whichever way you prefer to put it, employs more people than any other single employer in this country. At least, if there is another who employs more I do not know who it is. As has been pointed out today, by various members, I would say that in the last three years suspicion of the government among civil servants has been growing. Because of the delay and procrastination with respect to raising the salaries of civil servants and bringing them up to what they should be to meet the current cost of living we saw a very strong development among civil servants who started working together to present a united front to the government in support of their requests. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena, I think the method of giving increases to certain groups and taking other groups under consideration was devised for the sole purpose of breaking up that solid front. I do not know whether they are taken under consideration or under active consideration but I saw definitions of these two phrases the other day that I think are quite appropriate. I am sure many civil servants will agree with them. The definition of "under consideration" is "we never heard of it" and the definition of "active consideration" is "we are looking in the files for it".
I was never a civil servant but I spent
II	years of my life as a civic servant and there is really not too much difference between the two. I found from personal experience that it was six years after I started to work for the municipality before I enjoyed the same rights as I had enjoyed before entering

the service. It was not until after I had been with the department for six years, five of which I had spent actively in the trade union movement, that we were able to incorporate into our contract a grievance procedure sufficient to protect the members of that local and give them the same rights as everyone else.
Unfortunately these rights have not yet been passed on to the civil servants. They are still in the category of second class citizens. I recall when I first started to take an active part in politics I was warned by well-meaning friends that this was a crazy thing to do; you are going to lose your job. Well, I did, and I sometimes wonder if I improved my lot. The fact still remains that the civil servants of this country have not the same rights as other citizens of this country or as the employees of other employers. It seems that in every country there is a certain class which does not enjoy full citizenship. In India there are the untouchables, in South Africa there is apartheid and in Canada we have the civil servants.
I must confess that I was shocked when I came to Ottawa to realize that for the first time I had the power, without any proof required beyond my say so, to deprive any civil servant of his livelihood. I merely had to state that I knew he had taken an active part in politics. As I say, Mr. Chairman, 1 was shocked because I do not believe I have any right to that privilege, if you can call it a privilege. Certainly there is no other group of employees in this country whose jobs depend upon the whim of any one of 265 people. It is for this reason, Mr. Chairman, that I should like to support the plea of the hon. member for Skeena that when we are conducting a major overhaul of the Civil Service Act we should realize that the civil servants of this country are entitled to the same rights and privileges as any other citizens of this country. These rights should be guaranteed to them.
I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West, and with other hon. members, who have pointed out that at this late stage in the session, at a time when the annual speed-up has been put into operation, it is no time to start a major overhaul of the act in the hope of getting it passed at this session. I say that during this major overhaul we should give the rights to our civil servants that are granted to every other citizen of Canada and, in addition, we should devote the time necessary to make sure that the job is properly done.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity to make a few remarks
Civil Service Act
in connection with this resolution. It is obviously important, for the good administration of this country, that employees and employer be on excellent terms.
Everybody will agree that each civil servant, whatever his job, plays an important part in the administration. It is no sin for a man to labour in his vocation, whether it be in the public service or in other fields of human endeavour. Due allowance being made, the humblest of civil servants, is as necessary to an efficient operation of the government machine as the one occupying the highest post, which means that the man in charge of maintenance in public buildings, the elevator operator, the junior clerk doing some obscure and unassuming work, are quite as essential to this country as the highest state official. If people in the humblest of jobs do not play their part with a full sense of responsibility, the whole administrative machine can be impaired.
The civil servant obviously has some rights, but he also has responsibilities.
He has a right to expect some consideration on the part of his employer and to a treatment consistent with human dignity. He has a right to working hours enabling him to fulfil his obligations to the extent demanded by his employer. He is entitled to a salary that will allow him to face his personal and social obligations; in a word, he is entitled to a square deal.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that this government is prepared to entertain the fair and reasonable claims of public employees in the matter of salary increases.
But the government is expected to restore within a few weeks, or a few months, a balance which had been upset during the too many years of Liberal rule. Yet, it would be wrong to believe that living costs in this country increased spontaneously, or all of a sudden. If today, federal civil servants' salaries are out of line with the cost of living, it means that there was a lack of the necessary gradual adjustment. The best proof is found in the speech made by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) on January 25, 1960, when he said:
Some civil servants, because they receive an inadequate salary, have to take other employment in their spare time.
Mr. Chairman, I would not want to press this point unduly, but if civil service salaries

Civil Service Act
were inadequate a few months ago, why did not the former administration at the time immediately decide to remedy the position; because, as I said before, the cost of living cannot change and rise all of a sudden, in a single month, or even in a single year. It is a gradual process.
Consequently it must be recognized that in respect of salary increases for the civil service, this government has made a commendable effort to date.
Mr. Chairman, I was just now speaking of the civil servant's rights. Obviously, he has not only rights; he also has duties. And, before insisting on the civil servant's duties, I want to call your attention to the fact that our country is endowed with a system of government of which we are proud, that is the democratic system. As you know, some countries waged, and are still waging, a violent struggle to attain a system of government which ensures freedom to each and every citizen of a country, in accordance with human dignity as we understand it, that is in the Christian meaning of the term.
Under that system, the voice of the people has to be heard and understood by the government. The spokesmen for the people are, of course, the citizens who have been chosen and elected by them, and they are called members of parliament. In their respective communities, those members consider the problems and needs of the people, first through their personal studies and observations, as well as through social agencies that study problems of a sociological character, problems therefore of general interest, for the common weal. In reference to those social agencies, I should like to take this opportunity to draw the attention of the house to the fine contribution made in the form of the very substantial reports coming from the various sections of the chambers of commerce throughout Canada.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, the point I wish to make here is that the democratic system must allow the people to directly influence the conduct of the country's business, allowing them at the same time to guide their political destiny. That is why everything must be done to protect that system of government, so that there may always be, between the people and the government, easy communications as well as frequent and continuous relationships.
The purpose of my brief remarks is simply to point out to distinguished members of this house, wherever they sit, a danger which might make our democratic system inoperative and inefficient.

To put it briefly, Mr. Chairman, among the duties of civil servants towards the government, there is loyalty towards the representatives elected by the people. Otherwise, the civil service would eventually set up an impassable barrier between the government and the people. I am not complaining, Mr. Chairman, of the situation which might have existed in the past or which might now exist; I am making those remarks merely to describe what should be done in my opinion, to safeguard our system of government.
Consequently, civil servants must show great loyalty towards the representatives who have been elected by the people, and give evidence of serious co-operation.
If, after an election is held in Canada, civil servants were to apply laws already enacted by parliament without taking into account the directives or policy of the newly elected representatives of the people, well, as I said a moment ago, democracy would become inoperative, the voice of the people that is, the voice of those who have been vested with the responsibility of administering the country would never be heard.
Mr. Chairman, that is the danger I wanted to point out. I would not like to give examples nor lay any specific charge against anyone, but I say that it is a danger which any government must avoid, regardless of its political creed.
The government is responsible for seeing that the specific mandate entrusted to a member of parliament by his constituents is carried out, and division heads should follow that directive.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that in its amendments to the Civil Service Act, the present government will do something specific and practical about bilingualism and its application throughout Canada, and particularly in the various government departments.
On the matter of bilingualism, the government deserves credit for its practical action in this field. I do not want to take up too much of the house's time to list the government's accomplishments but let me mention the simultaneous interpretation system in the House of Commons-

Mr. Chairman, the matter before us is not controversial and it is one with which everyone here will I am sure agree. I agree with what the hon. member for Ottawa West said this afternoon; he dealt with the subject more extensively than I propose to. We can also agree with a lot of what the hon. member for Carleton said, although he dealt with the subject in a rather general way without pinpointing any real important changes in the act.
I have no doubt whatever that some amendments to the Civil Service Act are due and perhaps the act should have been considered for revision long before this. What appears to me to be wrong in bringing this measure up for discussion at this late date is the time factor involved in order to give these proposed changes the consideration they properly deserve.
Here is an important piece of legislation brought in in a late rush hour fashion as though we were dealing with merchandise instead of the welfare of an important segment of every community in Canada, with the possible exception of the rural areas. Any contemplated changes to the act should have been made known to parliament at the beginning, not when the talk is that the end of the session is a few weeks away.
One of the changes needed to bring this act up to date is that of giving civil servants the right to bargain with their employer. The Prime Minister, speaking at the merger banquet of the civil service association of Canada, made a statement which should foreshadow the application of the principle of bargaining rights. Said the Prime Minister:
I believe that civil servants, through their organizations, should have a greater voice ... in the process of determining ... and participating more effectively in the application of certain principles of policy ... There should be a more systematic

Civil Service Act
method of bringing your views and information to bear ... What is needed is more opportunity and better arrangements for your representatives to sit down at a table with officials representing the government and with officers of the civil service commission... You will have noticed I spoke of your representatives having a greater voice and participating more effectively in the application of certain principles of policy ... Your power will he the power of persuasion... Your success will depend, as it should, upon the merits of your arguments and the skill of your representatives in presenting them ...
Finally, perhaps the most important victory of them all so far, for you, was acceptance, free and full, by the government of the principle that it must lead the way in mutually rewarding, forward looking staff relations ... that is, people must be paid at least on a par with the best in competing fields of business and industry-
From this excerpt of the Prime Minister I wish to underline the passage where he said:
What is needed is more opportunity and better arrangements for your representatives to sit down at a table with officials representing the government and with officers of the civil service commission ...
If this sentence means what it is supposed to convey, then the Prime Minister is certainly committed to giving the civil service bargaining rights.
The issue is a simple one. It is whether or not a man or a woman working for the government should be deprived of those rights which are fundamental in our Canadian way of life. They want the right to sit at a bargaining table with their employers, the right to complain through newspapers or other media without fear of being dismissed, and the right to enter a committee room of a candidate for public office or to attend a political meeting without suffering the consequence of being cast in the ranks of the unemployed because of the whim of a member of parliament. Without these rights being clearly defined there would not be much use in rewriting the act.
Last November the hon. member for Winnipeg South, speaking at a meeting of Manitoba federal government workers, made the statement that he would give very serious consideration to the introduction of a bill in parliament to grant collective bargaining rights to civil servants. He later qualified the statement that he would bring the matter up in the caucus of the Conservative party and be guided by the general reaction of his colleagues. I think he was sincere, but evidently his colleagues were not impressed or he was prevented by the government from introducing a bill. If we are not going to make a better job the people will certainly feel that the government has let them down on a principle of which the Prime Minister has so often proclaimed himself its champion.
Arbitrary treatment of civil servants, however unintentional, should have no place in

any code of government conduct, and the civil service commission's annual recommendations should be tabled in parliament regardless of the nature of the recommendations.
In the matter of dealing with the question of salaries the Prime Minister made the following statement in May 1958:
For many years it has heen generally accepted that two main principles should guide the determination of salaries in the service.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was reading a statement made by the Prime Minister in May of 1958. He said:
For many years it has been generally accepted that two main principles should guide the determination of salaries in the service. First, the salaries must be enough to do the job, that is to attract enough of the right kind of men and women into the service and keep them in it; second, they must be fair as between civil servants and people outside the service, the taxpayers if you will, which means that the salaries we pay for any class of work should be comparable with those paid by private employers for similar classes of work, taking into account the other terms of employment that are necessary to make a fair comparison. 1 think these principles should continue to guide us.
He then went on to say:
We are fortunate in having in the commission persons of outstanding ability and long standing records of outstanding work as career civil servants with a wide variety of experience.
These are statements with which we all agree but unfortunately these principles have not been made operative at any time since they were enunciated two years ago. Civil service employees give of their best to the government of the day no matter whether a Conservative or a Liberal administration is in power and indeed that is the way it should be because after all the government of the day is elected by the Canadian people, the actual employers of the civil servants. In other words, they do not serve a particular political party but simply perform their duties to the best of their ability by serving and advising those in authority above them what is best for the Canadian people.
It is in the light of these considerations that I believe the civil servants should be treated. The treatment accorded them should be on a par with the treatment accorded those employed in other fields of endeavour by private industry as has already been indicated by previous speakers participating

in the debate this afternoon. Without these principles fully spelled out any changes in the act will be relatively meaningless.
These men and women of the civil service fully realize their responsibilities as part of the government's administration. Let us treat them not as machines but as our worthy partners working together each in our own sphere for a better and more prosperous Canada.

there is one matter which was touched on this afternoon by the hon. member for Ottawa West upon which I should like to comment. It had to do with the procedure on the bill with respect to the present session.

The hon. member for Ottawa West seemed to confuse this proposed detailed study with some suggestion of haste. There is nothing in my remarks this afternoon that bears that interpretation. My emphasis was on the necessity for the most careful consideration and study. I realize that that may take some time. That is something that will depend upon the length of time that the committee is prepared to devote day by day to this measure.
The hon. member asked me if in my opinion it was possible for the committee at the present session to give to this measure that detailed study. I expressed my own opinion on the subject and stated that that opinion based on a study of the act was that it could be done. No one knows the duration of this session, but the time required by this bill depends to some extent on the committee itself. I said, and I think rightly, that this is a matter for a decision of the house. I was giving an opinion on the point in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West.
Mention has been made of the fact that the various civil service associations will
Civil Service Act
wish to be heard. I am quite sure they will. The cabinet committee that was engaged on this subject heard representatives of the associations, and I am quite sure they will wish to be heard before the committee.
What I should like to appeal for is that hon. members suspend their judgment in this respect until they have seen the bill. Nothing could have been more admirable than the general sentiment expressed by the hon. gentleman that we should approach this matter in a non-partisan sprit. But I do hope that the house and the committee from now on will follow those precepts and not the example of the hon. member for Carleton who, having enunciated those lofty principles, proceeded to give a very thorough demonstration of how widely one can deviate from principles and still appear to be following them.
The hon. gentleman, of course, in talking about the ancestry of this legislation had something to say which, if I were to make a very poor pun I would say was somewhat a foreshortening of history because, as the hon. member for Carleton must know, with the erudition we all know he is so celebrated for, it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Dr. Adam Shortt who were really responsible for laying the foundations of the Civil Service Act. Mr. A. K. MacLean, when he introduced the motion in 1918, had this to say at page 699 of Hansard of April 12, 1918:
A few moments ago I stated that I did not think the great advance proposed by the terms of the order in council in the civil service of this country could have been accomplished by the leader of the opposition,-
I have not done a great deal of research, and this is an inference. I take it this was an order in council that had been passed under the War Measures Act by the union government. He went on to say:
-if he were in power as leader of the Liberal party,-
That would be Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
*-nor by the present prime minister-
That is Sir Robert Borden.
-if he were in office as head of the Conservative party. I did not intend to detract-
I draw the hon. gentleman's attention particularly to this sentence:

I did not intend to detract in the slightest from the credit due to the ministry led by my right hon. friend-
That is Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
-the leader of the opposition for passing the Civil Service Act of 1908. On the contrary, X think that ministry is entitled to every possible credit for passing that act. It was a great reform.
