speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman familiar with the quotation from Mr. A. D. P. Heeney, his predecessor as clerk of the privy council, which says that the Civil Service Act of 1918 gave Canada the greatest measure of public service reform existing anywhere in the world?

subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Oh, quite. I am also very familiar with the fact that Mr. A. K. MacLean never called himself a Conservative and that it was Mr. A. K. MacLean who introduced this legislation as a member of the union government. This does bring me to another aspect of this matter, and that is the motion which was introduced by Mr. MacLean. I think perhaps it might be worth while to put the terms of that motion on the record because I want to say something about the point that came up earlier today, Mr. Chairman, when you were not in the chair. The motion read:
Resolved, that It is expedient to consolidate, revise and amend the Civil Service Act of Canada: and to provide that the salary of the chairman of the civil service commission shall be six thousand dollars per annum; and to make provision for the readjustment of grades and salaries in the various classes of the inside service, and for the preparation by the commission of schedules of the positions, duties and salaries of the outside service or of any portion or branch thereof; and to make appointments to the public service upon competitive examination and otherwise eliminate political patronage in the control and management of the said service.
I read that for this reason: That resolution bears a marked dissimilarity to the resolution which is now before the committee and I want particularly to draw your attention, sir, to the dissimilarity between that resolution and the resolution which is now before us.
Perhaps when I have the attention of the Chair I can continue with this point. The resolution in 1918 spelled out very specifically

the charges upon the crown which were involved in this matter. It is a marked contrast, therefore, with the resolution which is now before us which says:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the civil service of Canada to amend, revise and consolidate the Civil Service Act, chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952.
During the course of this debate, I made * a very hasty examination of the act as it was recently consolidated and I could find nothing in the present act which appears to me to lay any charge upon the crown. Before the committee completes its consideration of this resolution the Minister of Finance should tell us what this resolution is really all about because the citation which was read this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, which I think ought to be put on the record again, namely citation 277 of Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, is very clear. It reads:
A bill, which does not involve a direct expenditure but merely confers upon the government a power for the exercise of which public money will have to be voted by parliament, is not a money bill and no resolution is necessary as a condition precedent to its introduction.
It has always been clearly understood that in these resolutions there is no harm in putting in much surplus verbiage, but the one thing that must be in the resolution is a precise statement of the charge which the crown is asking to be imposed. No bill can be introduced imposing a charge unless the preceding resolution which has been accepted by the house states precisely what that charge is. There is absolutely nothing in this resolution which states what is the charge upon the crown.
It is true that at one time up until a very few years ago the salaries of the civil service commissioners were set out in the act but that is no longer the case. They are now fixed by the governor in council. I believe hon. gentlemen who are on the treasury benches took exception to that legislation at the time it was passed and it may be that the minister in his bill is considering going back to the situation that prevailed before that amendment was made. But I would point out that if that is what he is doing he should have spelled it out in his resolution and that the bill cannot be considered by the house if it contains such a provision unless there has been a message from the crown to that effect.
Unless the government is deliberately anxious to prolong the session, one wonders why this resolution is on the order paper at all and being debated if there is no charge, and if there is a charge being imposed by
Civil Service Act
the legislation why the government has not spelled it out in the resolution. It seems to me that mystery should be cleared up by the minister before we complete consideration of this matter.
I should also like to refer to an editorial which I will not attempt to read because I know the minister can read and also because I am afraid I would be provoking the minister into rising on another of his frequent points of order if I did so. But before the minister rises perhaps I may go the length of commending to his attention an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of Monday, June 20 which says:	"Sane and balanced study of Civil
Service Act is essential". I think that is what is required if we are going to take our duties in the house seriously in a matter which is as serious as anything that is likely to come before us, as the hon. member for Carleton so justly indicated earlier today.
The government of this country under modern conditions cannot possibly function without an effective, reliable, honest and in the main I would go so far as to say a contented civil service. We cannot expect to have that unless we have the kind of legislation which gives to them a status, working conditions and a reasonable security which they have enjoyed in the past and to which I think every hon. member feels they are and should be entitled. I do not think it would be reasonable to consider that we should start on the 106th day of the session to attempt to pass at this session an act of parliament of the importance and of the volume of this legislation. There are things, of course, that are of the utmost importance but also of the utmost brevity but this matter is important without being brief and it cannot be made brief in any respect whatsoever.
Without prejudging the case, because I think we should all accept what the minister has said and look at the bill before we reach a final judgment on the matter, I would feel that the weight of evidence should lead us to reach the judgment that we should not proceed until everyone who is interested, including all civil service organizations and many other persons and organizations who have nothing to do with the civil service but are deeply concerned about good administration and good government of the country, has had adequate time to study the legislation and to make such representations as they may wish to make in order that when we revise and codify the act once again we will have the best possible legislation that we can, by the application of all our talents in a nonpartisan way, give to the Canadian people.

subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would not pretend to emulate the righteous indignation

Civil Service Act
expressed by the hon. member for Hull or the rolling, rollicking eloquence of the hon. member for Carleton, but I do want to take advantage of the latitude allowed at the resolution stage to deal particularly with one point that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and the Prime Minister. Before doing so, may I say that we wholeheartedly concur in the criticism of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on two particular points. First of all, this is most important legislation that concerns the people of Canada, the government of Canada and the civil service of Canada upon which efficient government has to depend. We think it is most unfortunate that this important and lengthy legislation has been introduced in the house at this late date in the session. I do not see how it can be properly dealt with unless the house is willing to sit until toward the end of August.
Second, we agree with his criticism-I had already looked up the same reference that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned-that the resolution is very barren indeed of information and of details concerning what the proposed act is going to include. However, we will have to leave our discussion of the details until we see the bill.
Others in this group and other hon. members of the house have dealt with the questions of collective bargaining rights for civil servants, terms of employment, classifications, salaries and so on. However, I want to take this opportunity to deal with a particular problem that I think is of interest to people who are first of all interested in an efficient civil service and also in the rights of the civil servants. When one reads the history of developments in Great Britain, France and other European countries he sees that there is a changing climate and a changing opinion in that direction. In speaking of the civil service this evening there may be a tendency to assume that such organizations are of long duration and have a considerable history. As a matter of fact, in terms of history a civil service is a very recent innovation on the part of parliaments and governments.
I checked up quite hurriedly in the library and found that the first indication of concern for a civil service by the British government was around 1848 to 1850. It is interesting to note that a civil service in all countries began to develop with the advance of industrialism and, shall I say, the fading away of feudalism or the remnants of feudalism because an industrial society requires first of all a better functioning government and therefore a more efficient and better functioning civil service.

Of course, under feudalism and the remnants of feudalism most government appointments were the result of nepotism and, as one might say, by grace.
I found that the first study was around 1848 to 1850. Then there was the Trevelyan Northcote report of 1853 which dealt extensively with the question of establishing a civil service in Great Britain. It was on the basis of that report that in 1870 Gladstone, by order in council, introduced the first civil service legislation in Great Britain. Since that time, of course, there has been tremendous development in the civil service of that country. As a matter of fact, it is so efficient that it has been a model for all other countries.
Coming to Canada I find on checking the records that the first civil service act of a rather primitive nature was passed in 1882. Then there were amendments in 1883, 1884 and 1885 which, according to my rather quick checking of the records, concerned largely what was then known as the inside civil service. You might say it was the birth of the civil service in Canada. But the great step forward was in April of 1918. Without doubt, for the first time in Canadian history the civil service was put on a sound foundation so far as legislation was concerned.
It interested me, in just checking the history of the past, to notice the recurrence of human weakness. I do not blame any party. This conception of to the victor belongs the spoils is a very human one. I can well understand that when a party has been out of power for 22 years it must have a considerable percentage of supporters who think it is their turn. Life is a rather short affair, and when you have not had a dip into the basket in 22 years you get a bit hungry. I am quite sure this government has had to resist a great deal in that respect because this is a very human weakness. The more civilized people become, the more they recognize what democracy really means, the more they are able to resist.
I was very interested in noting that in the debates of 1918, shortly after the union government was elected, there were still members of the Conservative party who, according to their correspondence, supported the idea of patronage. I should like to quote from Hansard for April 12, 1918, page 711, on which page a letter is to be found which reads as follows:
Dear Sir.
Yours of the 9th instant duly received. As far as any patronage in connection with the railway department is concerned, there is not the slightest doubt hut that both Liberals and Conservatives who supported the Union government will receive every consideration.

In fairness I must say that at the same time and in the same debate there is evidence that members of the same party had taken the very opposite point of view. I mention that to indicate that this is a human weakness which is found in all parties and because it is human, it is natural, we have to resist it.
When I was reading that I was reminded of a story. My father, who was president of the Liberal association of that day in the riding from which I come, actually supported the Union government. This was the only time he ever supported a hybrid thing in his life, and he did so on account of the war effort. I remember running through some correspondence in 1917 when this Conservative government was proposing these amendments to this Civil Service Act, and there was still this spirit of patronage. There was a Conservative association in our riding. This shows how a division can occur even within a party.
The president of the association was a strong patronage man and the secretary treasurer was an anti-patronage man. The secretary was pressing the association to support what the government intended to do, and so there was a clash. The president wrote to the minister of the day who was directly connected with British Columbia and told him about the difficulty he was having with the secretary. In fact, the president mentioned that the secretary thought he was living in England where you could run a government without patronage. The complaint was very bitter. The person to whom he was writing was not in sympathy with his ideas. This is what he wrote back. He said, My dear Mr. So-and-So: I fully appreciate your criticism of Mr. So-and-So, the secretary, but we are going to have an election within a few months and we do not want any trouble in the party.
To give you an idea that this man was very much against the whole idea, I may say he simply wrote, so far as I am concerned, we do not want any trouble within the party, so my advice to you is to continue to scratch his back until the election is over and then after that you have my permission to tell him to go to hell. This patronage condition within parties is something about which we all have to be watchful, no matter to what party you belong.
I want to deal now particularly with a point I raised, and bring it to the attention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. I refer to the question of the rights of civil servants, that is to have the full rights of citizenship. As I said before, this concerns thinking people. It has been mentioned before today. It is a matter of concern to
Civil Service Act
those who desire the maintenance of an efficient civil service and who, at the same time, want to see those civil servants given their full rights as citizens of the country. I want to bring to the Prime Minister's attention a book written by H. J. Laski entitled, "Reflections on the Constitution, the House of Commons, the Cabinet, the Civil Service", published by the Manchester University press. We all know Mr. Harold Laski as a Labour member of parliament and a very brilliant person.

subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext: He was never a member of parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENT, REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Excuse me, a lecturer at the London school of economics and chairman of the Labour party. I do not know why I made that slip. His writings are even read by Conservatives in England because he had a brilliant mind and was an authority on the constitution and parliamentary practices. I want to read a few paragraphs from this book because I believe that every thinking person who has given any thought to this problem- it is not an easy problem-will recognize that he does bring forward some very valid ideas. I think this is something to which consideration should be given. This chapter is headed, "The political rights and social interests of civil servants", and he says:
I turn to a very different issue-now a matter of acute controversy-on which I think far more clear and frank thought is necessary than it has thus far received-I mean the degree to which we ought to place restrictions on the political rights of civil servants.
Then farther down he says:
Above all, I believe it is a great mistake to separate the vast majority of officials from work in local government where, very often, their experience of administration would enable them to make an important contribution to the standards of administration. I do not believe that the public would lose confidence in the detachment and loyalty of civil servants if, under agreed conventions, they were given the chance of exercising the rights of a citizen.
Then he goes on to say:
In the French system, a great many civil servants, of whom, perhaps the best known among those living is that eminent humanist, Mr. Leon Blum, have played their part in politics without any deterioration in their work; and I have known scores of lesser cases in which the official's political affiliation was both active and known without producing the conviction that he would not be loyal to a minister whose convictions were of a different school.
I realize that when you get that type of relationship you have to have very high principles and devoted persons on both sides of the question.
Let me begin by saying that officials do not need a special party connection in order to make their views obvious.

Civil Service Act
Then he goes on at some length and says: .Perhaps I may summarize this by saying that when an official had strong political opinions, he could not conceal them from any but the most stupid of ministers for more than the first hour of their relationship; and the real question was, and is, granted those convictions, was he capable of looking at the minister's views with detachment, and of helping him to apply them with the full energy of his mind. The answer is, sometimes yes, and sometimes no. Sir Austen Chamberlain, in his autobiography, tells an admirable story of the permanent secretary of the post office when he was postmaster general.
I am sorry to see that the Postmaster General has just gone out, but I am sure his parliamentary secretary will listen to this.
They quarrelled violently over a decision Sir Austen proposed to make until at last he told his official that he had made up his mind that the decision stood. Thereupon, Sir Austen tells us, his permanent secretary said, "Well, Postmoster General, if you want to make a damn fool of yourself, I cannot prevent you from doing so. But at least I can show you how to do it with the least possible damage to the country."
Now there was a first class civil servant. I hope the minister's civil servants take the same attitude when required.
That is what I mean by loyalty and detachment, and I think they are qualities quite distinct from political convictions and party preference.
Farther down, he says:
First, it is clear that all members of the administrative class should impose upon themselves a self-denying ordinance in the political sphere.
I agree with that.
They ought to resign if they want to be candidates for parliament. They ought not to make political speeches. They ought not to write books or articles on the immediate issues of political controversy. They are too near the centre of power to do any of these things.
Then he goes on to say:
But below the administrative class, 1 do not think that rule should apply. It is enough if an official in the executive, or clerical class, give an undertaking, whether he becomes a parliamentary candidate or takes an active interest in his party, not to discuss in public the affairs of the department to which he belongs, nor to reveal information which he obtains by virtue of his position in the service; if he were to break his undertaking the permanent secretary would be justified in recommending disciplinary action, though I should hope that, before the permanent secretary made his proposal to the minister, he would discuss it with the departmental Whitley council and proceed, if possible, with its approval. I should give officials who became parliamentary candidates leave, with pay, for the period of their election. If they were defeated, they would return to the department in the ordinary way. If they were elected, I should put them on a special list the officials on which would be free to return to the department if they were defeated in the next election in their old grade, and with any increments of pay which had normally accrued to them; if. however, they were returned for a second parliament, I should assume that this operated as a normal resignation from the service, though I should hope that they would receive a due proportion of the pension rights they would

have received on retirement. I frankly see no difficulty in this. I do not really think such a candidature would embarrass the department. And if it is a question of practical activity other than that of a candidate, I feel pretty certain that no Manchester constituency would be seriously concerned about the fairness of civil servants if, let us say, a woman shorthand typist in the area office of the ministry of health made a swinging attack in the exchange division at a Tory meeting on the folly of Mr. Strachey's ground-nuts scheme, or a clerical officer in the office of the local inspector of taxes spoke with some heat about the refusal of the Home Secretary to ban the Fascist party. Assuming that the average civil servant observes the normal decencies of political behaviour, I am unable to believe that the liberation of the grades below the administrative would shock any public opinion or do any harm to the work of these departments.
He goes on at some considerable length, and then towards the end of his remarks he has this to say:
There are two related questions upon which I should like to say a word. I hope we shall rapidly end the system which prohibits the civil servant from writing upon politics and public administration save by the permission of the department. Here again my view is that there should be the right to freedom limited only by some obvious conventions which could easily be agreed through discussions in the Whitley organisation at national and departmental levels. I do not think that an official of the Foreign Office should attack his minister-
And so on. Anyway, he goes on to deal with the argument that, under proper central arrangements and under proper legislation, with a civil service of high standard it should be possible for civil servants below the administrative class to be allowed leave to take an active part in politics without losing their rights in the civil service until after, say, the second election.
I have mentioned these few quotations. I bring this book to the attention of the Prime Minister and the minister because he has given great thought to this matter. There has been discussion in the House of Commons in Great Britain. It has been given serious consideration and considerable attention. Mind you, as I have mentioned previously, the standards with respect to the treatment by ministers of the senior officials is very high indeed and is a model to the world. But in fairness to the civil service I think we should give some consideration to this question. To that end I urge the government of the day to consider this important question.
I frankly admit it is not a simple or an easy one. However, it is important to the people of Canada as a whole who are interested in an efficiently functioning civil service. It is important to the government that needs the continuing support of a first class civil service. It is also extremely important to the civil servants of Canada who are citizens of this country.

I trust the government and the committee will also give consideration to the other suggestions brought to the attention of the committee by various hon. members who have spoken in this debate this afternoon.

I am rising on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. As Your Honour will observe, the resolution on which the bill is to be founded, contains only the barest citation of the fact that the bill proposes to consolidate or revise the Civil Service Act. As Your Honour well knows, the purpose of a resolution preceding a bill is to indicate
Civil Service Act
clearly to the house the charge laid upon the exchequer by a money bill. As Your Honour is well aware, citation 277 of Beauchesne's fourth edition reads as follows:
277. (2) A bill, which does not involve a direct expenditure but merely confers upon the government a power for the exercise of which public money will have to be voted by parliament, is not a money bill and no resolution is necessary as a condition precedent to its introduction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is raising a point of order. In my submission to you this point of order is raised much too late. This afternoon the house by decision resolved itself into committee on this self-same resolution. That was a decision of the house. If any hon. member considered at that time that there was anything lacking in the resolution, that was the time to raise it. No such point was raised at the time. Hon. members are aware that such a motion is not debatable but it can be voted on; and if there is anything out of order about it a point can be taken, but it must be taken at the proper time. It is much too late now to be raising a point of this kind after the house has already resolved itself into committee on the resolution and the resolution has been reported back in pursuance of the instructions of the house. So I say in the first place that this point is raised much too late.
In the second place the hon. member is questioning whether this resolution is sufficient. He sought to raise the point this afternoon that the resolution did not go far enough, that it should have spelled out some provisions of the intended bill, or their effect, in greater detail. I do not think he can have it both ways.
It has been ruled, and I think it must be a matter of common knowledge in the house now, that the reason we have these resolutions involving charges or expenditure of

Civil Service Act
money is that the house shall have notice of the purpose of the measure. There have been statements and rulings to that effect. It is not necessary that the proposed charge be spelled out in specific terms. The hon. member before the committee rose sought to go back and raise these subjects again, or at least discuss them, although the point had been disposed of this afternoon.
I say in the first place, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members are aware that these resolutions preceding so-called money bills are drawn by the most experienced authority on this subject in Canada; they are drawn by the law officer of the House of Commons. When the law officer of the House of Commons draws a resolution I think hon. members are entitled to prefer his opinion as to the necessity of such a resolution and as to the sufficiency of the resolution which he draws over the opinion of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). However, I suppose there is no harm in his trying.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the house has had resolutions in comparable form on previous occasions and they have been ruled to be quite sufficient. There is a decision made in this house, for example, on March 24, 1882. On that occasion Mr. McLelan-

May I review the procedure which brings us up to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). Earlier in the day the house accepted a motion to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider the resolution in question:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the civil service of Canada to amend, revise and consolidate the Civil Service Act, chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952.
That resolution was then considered by the committee of the whole and it has been reported to the house. The report, by vote of the house, has now been received. Then the motion that the resolution be concurred in was accepted. What followed was a motion by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for leave to present a bill based on the said resolution. At that point the resolution has been accepted by the house in committee and reported. It has been adopted and the matter before the house is whether the minister shall have leave to introduce a bill based on the said resolution.

As I understood the argument of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate the bill should be looked at before the house gives leave to its introduction. I personally do not see how that could be done. The house does not accept the bill by allowing it to be introduced. If any exception is to be taken to the contents of the bill as not being in accordance with the resolution, then it seems to me that exception must be taken after the bill has been introduced and when it is under consideration. Therefore, I fail to see how the point of order is properly taken at this time. It seems to me that the motion must be accepted or rejected.
When the bill is introduced, if it appears that the other matters which have been debated are relevant and there has been an insufficiency of resolution to support the bill, that point may be taken, of course, on any particular section of the bill which seems to go beyond the resolution improperly and it could be objected to on that ground.

I bespeak this aid for these young men and women who find it difficult to pay the increasing cost of school fees, whose parents of modest means cannot afford to pay for their education, but who could easily obtain assistance from corporations or perhaps from relatives of more comfortable means to pay for this education. Provision for that exemption, I suggest to the minister, would be a constructive piece of legislation to incorporate into our Income Tax Act, namely of all school fees of universities or other institutions of higher education. I am speaking of related seminaries or, if there are such things, technical schools that are considered to be on a higher level of education. By doing that I think the government would be enacting a popular piece of legislation. Not only would it be popular with the taxpayers but it would be in conformity with our genuine desire and urge for university education in Canada.
I make that as a suggestion to the minister. 1 do not see provision for it in this bill. I am wondering whether, between now and the time we reach clause by clause study of the bill, he will consider the introduction of such an amendment so that we might get into this act one section that would be more popular perhaps than are many of the sections that are now in the bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I remind the house that if the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) was not any clearer this evening than usual. However, he somehow said that taxes had been increased for the people who constitute the great bulk of the Canadian taxpayers. He was completely wrong. I propose to quote what I had to say on this subject in the budget speech of 1959. This is to be found at page 2417 of Hansard, of April 9, 1959, in the second column, where, summarizing the tax changes in the 1959 budget and comparing the income tax position of the great bulk of Canadian taxpayers with their tax position prior to the change of government three years ago tomorrow, I had this to say:
The best way to illustrate the effect on the individual is to compare the taxes which will be payable in a full year after this year's changes with the taxes payable in 1957 prior to the reductions we introduced in that year. For purposes of comparison, let us consider the position of a typical married man who is the father of two children of family allowance age.
At an income level of $3,000 a year, under the new rates, this man will pay a total of income 79951-0-3264
Income Tax Act
tax and social security contribution of $56, an increase of $4 from the 1958 level. He will, however, be paying $34 less than he paid before the reductions we introduced in 1957.
At an income level of $4,000 a year, under the new rates, he will pay a total of $208, an increase of $14 from the 1958 level but $44 less than before the reductions we introduced in 1957.
At an income level of $5,000 a year, he will pay a total of $390, an increase of $24 from the 1958 level but $44 less than before the reductions we introduced in 1957.
At an income level of $7,500 a year, he will pay a total of $898, an increase of $68 from the 1958 level but still $2 less than before the reductions we introduced in 1957.
It is clear from these examples that even after the increases now being proposed the vast majority of taxpayers will be paying less in income tax and old security contributions than they paid prior to the reductions we introduced in 1957.
At the same time they are receiving the protection of a social security system which has been greatly improved and extended.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River may find his way back to these facts some time soon. That will be our hope.
As to the matter raised by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), may I say that this matter was discussed fully last year. He is aware of the additional burden we are carrying in the federal treasury now by reason of our increase from $1 to $1.50 in the per capita federal grants to the universities; that is per capita of population in each province. These are substantial additions that we have undertaken. I think there is little to be gained now in reviewing this question again. It could have been raised in the budget discussion but I do not believe it was raised there. It was discussed fully a year ago and I think the situation has not changed since that time. The government has done more for the assistance of universities than any other federal government has ever before done in Canadian history.
May I ask the Minister of Finance a question?

Order. House in committee on Bill No. C-68, an act to amend the Income Tax Act and also the proposed amendments which are appended to Votes and Proceedings.

Income Tax Act
Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, on this clause I would like to refer back to page 4591 of Hansard, the explanation which I think is not now a fully responsible explanation for the Canadian public to be given by the Minister of Finance with respect to the intent of this legislation. Although I am sure the minister has read the debate in the other house on the Estate Tax Act, there was reference in the course of it to certain amendments such as those which are before us in this house. There was reference to the fact that the other place referred the amendments of 1958, certain proposals of the Minister of Finance, back to us. The over-powering majority in this house rejected them.
To what extent have we here a recognition of the non-political judgment that might have been exercised in the other place when they considered the elements involved in a matter of this kind?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
Well, is the minister not going to reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a political question. The hon. member has not asked for elucidation of this clause. I am prepared to offer to elucidate the clause if any hon. member asks.

Then we can go on for some time. Has the minister before him, and I am sure he has because his officials formerly always prepared a very excellent book of words clause by clause, any reference to what the recommendations were from the committee of the other house with respect to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we do not discuss what transpires in the other place; it is quite out of order to do so.
Mr. Chairman, I want to say we very definitely discussed what happened in the other place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the other house is dealing with a matter and sends it back to us, then this house deals with it. But with great respect we do not discuss the proceedings in the other place and it is quite out of order to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I am referring to the fact that last year we discussed the merits of a proposal that came from the other house. The overriding majority of the government defeated it here, but it seems to me it is back here before us. I wonder if the minister with the help of the staff that is in front of him would indicate
[The Deputy Chairman.)
to us to what extent this complies with the legislation that was presented to us last year which we rejected?
The Depuiy Chairman: Shall clause 1 carry?
Is the minister not going to assist the committee?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
there was no amendment last year to the Income Tax Act in this regard. If the hon. member wishes to talk about another act altogether, or about what happened with that other act last year, or what happened to a bill to amend that act this year in the other place, it is completely out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I would not have risen to say anything further had it not been for the fact that I am quite sure that very competent lawyers whose evidence I have read in committees of the other place have asserted that we are doing here, by means of the Income Tax Act amendment, what the other place suggested we should do when admittedly they had before them the Estate Tax Act. The two are related in the resolution now before us-
The Depuiy Chairman:	Order. I cannot
understand how the hon. member can show that what he is talking about is relevant to clause 1 of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, have you looked at the left hand sidenote, "Estate tax and succession duties-", which relates to this clause, and are you satisfied that I am not in order in asking about the co-relation between this clause and the legislation that was before this house last year?

I wonder if the minister might at this stage supply us with an answer as to why he has not included in the bill adequate amendments so that corporations would also be liable to graduated income tax, as are individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with respect, that question does not arise on this bill. The proper place to raise questions of this kind is in the budget debate which took place two months ago. There is nothing in this bill which relates to that subject at all.

On that point of order, Mr. Chairman, if clause 1 has any significance at all, I should be allowed to ask this. It always has had great significance in committee when we are amending the whole of an act to this great extent. I submit we ought to be entitled to ask this question, and it is the only place where we can ask the minister why the act has not been amended in other respects.
